  nanoseconds against the paced session's 2400. Two hundred and
  fifty-six pages puts them at 7400 and 7700.
- *The pages are a chain and not an array*, because two hundred and
  fifty-six addresses is two kilobytes and a kernel stack is four. Each
  page holds the address of the next and a byte of its own, so the walk
  carries no index of where it is going and the only memory it touches
  is the memory being measured. Walking a prefix of the chain is what
  makes the short pass the same walk over fewer pages.
- *What says the frames went back is the chain and not the frame count.*
  The first version compared `page_used()` before against `page_used()`
  after, which M13 stage four had already ruled out: the frame count is
  the whole machine's, the other core is running, and an assertion that
  it is exactly what it was is an assertion that nothing else moved a
  frame in the instant this looked. No boot failed that way, which is
  the point, since nothing would until one did. The free walk counts
  what it hands back and asserts that count instead, and that number is
  this check's own.
- *And every one of them can be false.* Taking both flushes out fails
  with "1327 ticks flushed against 1323 warm, which is not a cost",
  which is the whole margin gone. Recording the full walk as the short
  one fails with "1411 ticks over 256 pages against 1411 over 64, which
  does not grow". Taking the flush out of the short pass alone fails
  with "3000 ns over 64 pages is 718 a page and nothing for the flush".
  A walk that stops one page early reports "the walks read 4435032, not
  4445952", and one that walks the full chain where it should walk a
  quarter reports "the walks read 5483520, not 4445952". Leaking one of
  the frames reports "handed back 255 frames of 256".

**2. An identifier per space, and a switch that keeps its translations.**
*Built.*

- One field on `struct addrspace`, assigned when the space is created,
  written into the root register at activation, and the flush removed
  from that path. riscv64 first, because its entries are already tagged
  and the port needs the number rather than the entries changing.
- *The width is asked and not assumed.* Ones are written into the
  field and what stuck is read back, with the mode field left at zero so
  the probe cannot turn translation on or point it anywhere. Asked
  before the first space is built, which is the moment there is nothing
  in the register worth keeping. This host answers sixteen bits, so
  65535 spaces it can tell apart. A port that answers zero gets the old
  behaviour for every space, and that is how aarch64 still runs.
- *Zero is not an identifier, it is the absence of one.* A space holding
  it is activated by throwing every translation away, which is what
  makes it safe for several spaces to hold it at once. That is the
  fallback for a port with none to give and for a system that has run
  out, and it is what keeps the tree correct at this stage rather than
  at stage four.
- *Which entries are global: none of them, and the reason is a grant.*
  The plan said the kernel's identity map is the same in every space and
  so could be marked global, one copy for the machine instead of one per
  space. It is not the same in every space. `grant_unmap` says so in its
  own comment: a grant covers memory the kernel maps as well, so a
  process holding one has the kernel's own entry for that address
  rewritten with user access, in its space and no other. The console
  page is the standing example. An entry marked global is an entry
  claiming to be the same everywhere while a grant is busy making it
  not, so nothing is marked global and each space keeps its own copy of
  the kernel's translations.
- *Check.* Two spaces, one virtual address, two frames behind it, read
  from the kernel with interrupts off. The address is the base of the
  window programs live in, which is the one range no space maps for the
  kernel, so what answers there is what the space being asked put there.

  ```
  spaces: whether a switch keeps what it learned
      identifiers this port has              16 bits, 65535 to give
      the identifier the hardware ran under  41, then 42
      one address in two spaces reads        0xa1, 0xb2, then 0xa1 again
      switches that flushed everything       0 of 4
      a walk after a switch, and without one 131200 ns against 7900
  ```

- *And the flush count is asserted*, both here and over the whole boot.
  The report line M6's review put above the compared region now reads
  "address space switches: 5480, of which 7 threw every translation
  away, against 46 buffer halves" on riscv64 when this was written, and
  ten since stage six added a check that does maintenance of its own.
  aarch64 reads "5482, of which 5482". A port with no identifiers
  flushes on every switch, and a port with identifiers flushes on fewer
  and not on none: the seven are the review's doing and are explained
  below.
- *Removing the flush removed a guarantee nobody had written down, and
  the review is what found it.* riscv64's fences reach only the core
  that issues them, which the README has listed as a limitation since
  M13. What made it survivable was that every dispatch into a different
  address space threw the whole cache away, so a stale entry another
  core had already invalidated lived at most until this core's next
  switch. Stage two removed that flush and with it the accident, and an
  entry another core invalidated would have lived for the rest of the
  run. The concrete case is `grant_unmap`, which rewrites a page's entry
  to take user access away and flushes locally: on the other core the
  old entry, user access and all, would simply have stayed.
- *So the rule is now kept on purpose.* Each core counts the local
  maintenance it performs, a core reads the sum of the others, and the
  dispatcher throws everything away at its first switch after that sum
  moves. It reproduces the old guarantee exactly, no stronger and no
  weaker, and it cost seven flushes in a boot where the old rule cost
  5480. Read as the sum of the others and not as one counter for the
  machine, because a core that invalidated something is not the core
  still holding it; one counter costs 2546 flushes instead of seven,
  since most of this system's page faults are filled on the core that
  took them.
- *What that mechanism is not is cross-core maintenance*, which this
  kernel still does not have. It is the difference between an entry that
  survives a switch and one that survives the run.
- *And only half of it can be checked from one core.* That a core's own
  maintenance does not make it flush is checked and fails with "this
  core's own maintenance moved its own count, 70 to 71" if the counter
  is made global. That another core's maintenance reaches this one is
  not checked directly; what stands in for it is that the boot's flush
  count is not zero, which fails with "no switch threw anything away, on
  2 cores" if the counting is removed. Arranging the two cores on
  purpose is M19 stage five's, and that stage now owns this.
- *The read of two spaces cannot fail on this host, and that is the
  stage's real finding.* Dropping the identifier out of the value
  written to `satp`, so that every space runs under zero with no flush,
  changes nothing: both spaces still read their own page. QEMU discards
  every translation whenever the root register is written, tagged or
  not. So that check tests the emulator's caution and not this kernel's
  tagging, which is exactly the thing M19's own *Watch for* warned
  against and this project has now produced seven milestones running.
- *What can fail is what the hardware was told*, and that is checked
  instead: the identifier is read back out of the register rather than
  taken from the structure that was written into it. Dropping it from
  the value fails at once with "the hardware was running under 0 and 0,
  not 41 and 42". Giving both spaces the same one fails with "both were
  given identifier 1". Leaving the flush in fails with "4 of 4 switches
  flushed, with 16 bits".
- *And what the host does about it is measured, not asserted.* The same
  chain of pages walked twice, once without leaving the space and once
  having just entered another one: 131200 nanoseconds against 7900. A
  switch costs what a flush costs. The comparison that settles it is
  across the two ports, since aarch64 still flushes on every switch and
  answers 131056 against 8032. The port that stopped flushing and the
  port that did not are within a tenth of a percent of each other. On
  this host the identifier buys nothing, because the emulator throws its
  own translation cache away on every write of the root register.
- *That is a result and not a broken stage.* The kernel now performs no
  flush on a switch, which is a property of the kernel and is asserted.
  Whether a machine keeps anything because of it is a property of the
  machine, and the only machine this project runs on does not. M19's
  *Would falsify* asks whether identifiers are the cheaper way to buy
  what a cohort buys; the honest answer so far is that this project
  cannot measure the saving, and stage seven has to say so in those
  words rather than report a number it did not observe.

**3. The other port, and what the two do not share.** *Built.*

- aarch64 sets nG on every leaf it writes, puts the identifier in the
  top of `TTBR0_EL1` beside the root, and selects the width in
  `TCR_EL1.AS`.
- *The ports diverge here in a way worth writing down, and it is the
  whole of the difference.* On riscv64 the entries were tagged already
  and the port needed the number; on aarch64 the number was already
  writable and the entries had to stop calling themselves global. So on
  one port marking an entry global is an optimisation, and on the other
  it is what every entry already was. None is left global on either, for
  stage two's reason: a grant rewrites the kernel's own entry for the
  address it covers, in one space and no other.
- *Eight bits or sixteen is the hardware's to say, not the header's.*
  `ID_AA64MMFR0_EL1.ASIDBits` is asked, and sixteen taken when it is
  offered, because an identifier space that runs out has to be recycled
  and recycling is the expensive part. Asked of a register rather than
  written and read back, which is riscv64's method only because riscv64
  has no register that answers. The selection goes into `TCR_EL1` in
  `md_mmu_enable` and nowhere else, since that is the one place allowed
  to write the registers that describe the format, and both cores come
  through it.
- *Check.* The same two-space check on both ports at Tier 2, and the
  count of flushes removed is not merely comparable but identical.

  ```
  spaces: whether a switch keeps what it learned
      identifiers this port has              16 bits, 65535 to give
      leaves say which space they belong to  the program's and the kernel's
      the identifier the hardware ran under  41, then 42
      one address in two spaces reads        0xa1, 0xb2, then 0xa1 again
      switches that flushed everything       0 of 4
  ```

  That block is what both ports print, line for line. Over the boot,
  riscv64 reports 5480 switches with 7 flushes and aarch64 reports 5482
  with none. The seven are the other core's invalidations reaching this
  one, which aarch64 does not need because its fences are
  inner-shareable and reach the other core themselves. That is the
  second thing the two ports do not share, and it is the one that shows
  up in a number.
- *The stage's own work needed a check the stage did not have.* An
  identifier written into the root register while every leaf still calls
  itself global is a number nothing reads, and a system in that state
  boots, runs, and prints: every space would share every translation,
  and a cache that answers for the wrong space answers with the right
  page until two spaces disagree about one address. Neither the read of
  two spaces nor the read-back of the register would notice. So the
  descriptor itself is read back, at whatever level the port put the
  leaf, and asked whether it says the translation belongs to one space.
  Both ports answer the same question and spell it in opposite
  directions, which is why it is asked of the port.
- *And it can be false, four ways.* Leaving aarch64's leaves global
  fails with "the leaf for a program's page is not tagged". Dropping the
  identifier out of `TTBR0_EL1` fails with "the hardware was running
  under 0 and 0, not 41 and 42". Marking riscv64's kernel mappings
  global, which is what stage two decided against, fails with "the leaf
  for the kernel's own memory is not tagged". Leaving either port's
  fence in the switch fails with "4 of 4 switches flushed, with 16
  bits".
- *Both ports answering sixteen bits left the fallback unrun, and the
  review is what noticed.* Zero means the absence of an identifier, and
  a space holding it is entered by throwing every translation away.
  Nothing in a boot reaches that now, so the branch would have sat there
  until the day it mattered, which is the day identifiers run out. The
  check asks one space to hold zero and requires two things of it: that
  entering it flushes, and that it still reads its own page, since an
  identifier taken away is not a mapping taken away. Removing the flush
  from that branch fails on both ports with "entering a space with no
  identifier kept what it had".
- *The check was violating the contract it was checking.* `md_unmap`
  does no TLB maintenance and says so, and the check unmapped two
  spaces, destroyed them and handed their frames back without any. What
  that leaves is a translation to somebody else's memory, filed under an
  identifier nothing hands out twice yet. The last clause is the whole
  of why it did not matter and none of why it would be right to leave,
  and it stops being true at stage four.
- *And the width probe is a loaded gun on riscv64.* The way to ask is to
  write `satp`, so asking after translation is on writes mode zero into
  the register the kernel is running through and turns translation off
  in the middle of the sentence. Ordering in `vm_kernel_init` is what
  keeps that from happening, and the caller who gets it wrong is a
  caller added later. It is refused where it happens now: with the
  answer no longer remembered, the next spawn fails with "asid: asked
  how wide the field is with translation on" instead of the machine
  disappearing.
- *What the host still does not do is honour any of it.* The same chain
  walked twice, once without leaving the space and once having just
  entered another: 133152 nanoseconds against 7888 on aarch64, 131400
  against 8000 on riscv64. Writing the root register discards every
  translation on this emulator whichever port asks, so both ports now
  pay the same price for the same saving, which is none. The kernel is
  correct and the measurement is unchanged, and stage seven has to say
  both.

**4. Running out of identifiers, and the entry that outlives its space.**
*Built.*

- A name goes back to a list when its space is destroyed, and the next
  space built takes it. What makes that safe is one call: the
  translations filed under the name are thrown away where it is handed
  back, which is the place that knows nothing is running in the space
  any more. Both ports have an instruction that names a space rather
  than an address, and neither had been asked for it before.
- *The epoch that covered this is gone, which is what the stage was
  for.* A count of how many spaces had been destroyed used to force an
  activation at every core's next switch, and an activation flushed, and
  that flush is what actually cleared a stale cache. Stage two took the
  flush out and left the count a comparison that did nothing. It is
  removed, along with the per-core copy of it, and the dispatcher now
  compares the root and the name. A root is a frame and comes back, so a
  root is not by itself a space; a name is handed on, so a name is not
  by itself a space either. What makes the pair enough is that a name's
  translations are gone before any space can be built with it.
- *Reuse is not what a cap causes, which is a correction to this plan.*
  The plan said to cap the identifier space small enough for a boot to
  exhaust so that reuse would be reached. It is reached at any cap: a
  name goes back the moment its space dies and the next space takes it,
  so a boot hands 36 names on with a cap of 32 and hands the same 36 on
  with a cap of 4096. What the cap is really for is the list of names
  handed back, which is an array and has to be one, since a kernel that
  allocates in order to free is a kernel with a way to fail while giving
  something up. Thirty-two is above the number of spaces ever live at
  once, which is what keeps a space from having to run with no name.
- *Check.* One space is run in until the hardware has learned the
  address that matters, destroyed, and the next space built takes its
  name and maps a different frame at the same address. Reading it must
  give the new page.

  ```
  names: what a space inherits with a second-hand one
      one name, two spaces                   8, twice
      the same address in each of them       0xc3, then 0xd4
      names in use, of the cap               6 of 32, 36 given a second time
      taking every name there is             27 built, 1 went without
  ```

- *The read cannot fail on this host and the plan asked that it should,
  so the assertion is elsewhere.* The plan wanted the failure to be the
  wrong page rather than a fault, and on a host that honoured
  identifiers it would be. This one discards every translation whenever
  the root register is written, so a system that recycled a name without
  throwing anything away would read the right page anyway. What can be
  false is whether the kernel asked: the release is bracketed and the
  count of names thrown away must be exactly one. Removing the
  invalidation fails with "0 identifiers thrown away when one space
  died". Handing names back first-first instead of last-first fails with
  "the second space got 3, not the 8 the first handed back", which is
  the check losing its arrangement rather than the kernel losing its
  correctness, and is worth failing on for that reason.
- *And running out is reached on purpose rather than by crippling the
  cap.* Every remaining name is taken, and the space after that gets
  zero, which is not a name: it is entered by throwing every translation
  away, so any number of spaces may hold it and each is correct. That
  space still reads what it mapped, because a name it did not get is not
  a mapping it did not get. Then all of them go back and a further space
  gets a name again, which is the half of running out that a pool with a
  leak would fail. Twenty-seven spaces are built to reach it and one
  goes without.
- *Removing the epoch left a hole where the names run out, and the
  review is what found it.* Zero is not a name, so any number of spaces
  hold it at once, and once a root frame has been freed and handed out
  again two of them can have the same root as well. The dispatcher was
  comparing the root and the name, so it would have recognised the pair
  and skipped the entry, and one nameless space would have run through
  another's translations. The old epoch covered that and the new pair
  does not, which is the same class of gap the stage was written to
  close and one step further along. A space with no name is now entered
  every time, which is what having no name means.
- *And the rule that decides it had no way to be asked a question.* It
  was an `if` in the dispatcher, exercised thousands of times a boot and
  never on the two cases that matter: a space a core is already running
  in, which must be skipped or the whole saving is fictional, and a
  space with no name, which must be entered. Neither is reached by a
  boot, because a boot never builds two nameless spaces and never asks
  whether a skip was right. The rule is now a function the check asks
  directly. Recognising a nameless space fails with "a space with no
  name would not be entered, so two of them could share a core's
  translations". Entering every time fails with "a space a core is
  already running would be entered again". Ignoring the root and the
  name does not reach the check at all: the machine runs every program
  through the wrong translations and stops with "nothing interrupted a
  program in 20 runs of one", which is a system failing rather than a
  check reporting, and is the one of the three that says least.
- *Two smaller things.* A name handed back into a full list was dropped
  silently, which cannot happen, since every name is either out or on
  the list and the list is as long as there are names. It panics now,
  because a name quietly lost is one nothing can ever hand out again and
  nothing would say so. And both ports' invalidate-by-name leaves global
  entries alone, on riscv64 by the instruction's definition and on
  aarch64 by only reaching entries whose leaf said nG. That is correct
  only because stage two decided nothing would be global, and the two
  facts were three stages and two files apart. They are written down at
  the instruction now.
- *Noted and not changed.* A space built while the names are exhausted
  never gets one afterwards, because a name is assigned when a space is
  created and nothing hands one out later. On a machine that stays past
  a shortage, that space keeps flushing on every entry for as long as it
  lives. It is correct and it is slow, and making it otherwise means a
  space that can change its name underneath a running core, which is a
  larger mechanism than anything this milestone has needed.
- *Three more ways to be false.* A pool that never says it has run out
  fails with "32 spaces built and every one of them got a name". A pool
  that does not put names back fails, at the first check that wanted
  two, with "both were given identifier 0". Entering a nameless space
  without a flush fails with "entering a space with no identifier kept
  what it had".

**5. Two cores, one identifier space.** *Built.*

- *The ports differ, and until now nothing had asked the machine
  whether they do.* aarch64's invalidations are inner-shareable and
  reach the other core; riscv64's `sfence.vma` is local to the core that
  executes it, which is the standing limitation this project has carried
  since M13. Both are claims made in comments. This core changes what an
  address maps to, invalidates it, and the other core reads the address
  without having been dispatched in between, and what comes back says
  which kind of port this is.

  ```
  the other core: what it is still holding
      two readers on the other core          OK
      and the one that follows it            OK
      this port's fences reach               the core that issues them
      one address read three times there     0xf1, 0xf1, then 0xf2
  ```

  aarch64 prints "every core" and "0xf1, 0xf2, then 0xf2". The middle
  read is the whole check: the same kernel, the same arrangement, and
  two different answers because the two ports are different machines.
- *The port's claim is checked against the machine's behaviour, and
  neither is assumed.* What the check knows about the port is whether
  the invalidation moved this core's count of maintenance the other core
  has to hear about, which is what a port with local fences raises and a
  port with shareable ones does not. A port that raises it must leave
  the other core holding what it had; a port that does not must not. So
  a port that is wrong about itself fails here.
- *This is the one check in M19 the emulator will let fail.* Everywhere
  else it discards every translation whenever the root register is
  written, and hides the answer. Here nothing is written. Making
  aarch64's invalidation non-shareable while it still claims otherwise
  fails with "this port says its fences reach the other core, and that
  core read 0xf1", and so does making riscv64 stop saying its fences are
  its own.
- *What it cannot check is the rule, and three attempts established
  that.* The plan asked for the other core to read the new page after a
  dispatch, and for deleting the counting to make that read return the
  old one. It does not. The emulator holds a translation for a handful
  of instructions and loses it across a thread being dispatched,
  whatever the kernel does, so the read after a dispatch is right on a
  system with the counting removed and on a system without it. It is
  asserted anyway, as a statement that nothing else went wrong. The rule
  itself is checked where a rule can be checked, by asking it directly,
  which is what M19 stage four's review built it a function for.
- *And what the check itself costs, which the review had to measure
  rather than assume.* Both cores hold interrupts off across their half
  of the arrangement, and the first version had each of them wait inside
  that half for the other to be dispatched, which is a scheduler away.
  Core 0's longest interrupts-off region in a boot went from about 1200
  microseconds to about 10000, in two runs out of three, which is an
  order of magnitude worse than anything else this system does and is
  the number section 13.3 exists to bound. Waiting for the other core to
  be running is done outside the region now, and what is left inside is
  a handshake with a core already spinning for it and one entry written
  into a page table that already exists. Core 0 is back to about 900.
- *Core 1's longest region is now this check's, at about 450
  microseconds against about 250 before, and that is as short as it
  gets.* What is in it is two hart-to-hart handshakes, and each one
  costs whatever an emulator that interleaves its harts charges to make
  one hart's store visible to the other. Both are needed: the other core
  has to have read the address before this one changes it, and this one
  has to have changed it before the other reads again. It is a check's
  cost and not the kernel's, and it is reported where every other
  duration is, above the compared line.
- *A wait that runs out is a panic now, and was not.* The first version
  read the second time whether or not the change had happened, so a
  system too slow to make the arrangement would have compared two reads
  of the same page and said something about a port. Every wait here says
  what it was waiting for when it gives up.
- *And the maintenance count is sampled with interrupts off*, which it
  was not. What that count says has to be what this invalidation did,
  and a thread dispatched between the two readings could invalidate
  something of its own and make a port with inner-shareable fences look
  like a port without them.
- *And the check was wrong twice before it was right, both times in the
  same direction.* The first version had the second reader spin on
  `sched_yield()` waiting for a flag, and a thread that spins that way
  can be handed the core straight back without any switch having
  happened: it failed about one run in twenty, in the burst session,
  with the message it would print if the kernel were wrong. The second
  version let the first reader yield through the window between the
  change and the read, and anything dispatched there takes a page fault
  sooner or later, and filling a fault flushes the core that takes it.
  Both times the check was measuring the scheduler. What it does now is
  hold the other core with interrupts off across both reads, which is
  the only window the emulator gives.

**6. The buffer path, and whether M6's correction was right.** *Built.*

- *It was not right, and the buffer path did not change.* M6's review
  said that once entries are tagged, one invalidation stops covering
  both spaces and the buffer path needs two calls per page instead of
  one. Both ports have a by-address form that names no identifier and
  reaches every space, and that is the form the buffer path has always
  used, so a page moving between two spaces still needs one call. The
  compared report still says "46 invalidations" for 46 pages, on both
  ports and at both tiers, and that file is the assertion.
- *So the question became whether two calls that name the two spaces
  would be cheaper anyway*, which is a measurement and not an argument.
  The narrow form exists on both ports and had never been written: it is
  `sfence.vma va, asid` on one and `tlbi vae1is` with the identifier in
  the operand on the other. Both are built, and both are timed against
  the broad call over two spaces with the address really mapped in each,
  because an invalidation naming a space nothing holds is not the work
  being priced.

  ```
  a page moved: one call that names no space, or two that do
      what is invalidated                    1 pages, 128 times each
      one call naming no space               10387 ns
      one that names one space               10400 ns
      two that name the two spaces           20537 ns
      so a page moved is cheaper with        the one broad call
      naming this space drops its entry      yes
      naming another space drops it too      yes, so nothing here is narrower
  ```

  aarch64 answers 3134, 2978 and 7534. One narrow call costs what one
  broad call costs on riscv64 and slightly less on aarch64, and two of
  them cost twice, so on neither port is there a case for the buffer
  path to name its spaces.
- *Whether the narrow call does anything is asked, and whether it is
  narrow is only reported.* The review added the first: a call that
  dropped its argument on the floor would cost the same, come out of the
  comparison the same way, and invalidate nothing, so the address is
  mapped in the kernel's own space, read once to cache it, made to name
  a different frame, invalidated in the space that holds it, and read
  again. Taking the instruction out of either port fails with "naming
  this space read 0x11, not 0x22, so the narrow call reached nothing".
- *The second is reported because over-invalidating is legal.* An
  implementation may throw away more than it was asked for and stay
  correct, and both of these do: naming a space that does not hold the
  entry drops it anyway, on both ports. So the narrow form is not
  narrower here whatever the instruction means, which is the same thing
  the timings say from the other side. What is not the cause is the
  rewriting of the page table entry, which was tried: with the
  invalidation taken out, the second read still shows the frame the
  first one cached.
- *And what that says about the buffer path's own numbers is larger than
  the stage.* An invalidation of one address costs about 10400
  nanoseconds on riscv64, and stage one measured a whole-TLB flush at
  11252 plus 479
  for each page the next thread wants back. On this host, removing one
  address costs what throwing everything away costs. The buffer path's
  case for naming its addresses rests on the narrower call being
  cheaper, and on this emulator it is not, which is a fact about the
  emulator and is exactly the kind of thing stage seven has to say
  rather than report a saving nobody can see.
- *The counts are asserted and the durations reported, per M9*, and an
  empty run of the same length is timed beside them, because a loop of
  calls the compiler decided to drop would be the fastest of all of
  them. Removing the invalidation from the timed loop fails with a
  broad run no slower than an empty one.
- *Eight rounds a trial and not two hundred and fifty-six*, which is M19
  stage five's lesson arriving one stage later. At ten microseconds a
  call the longer run held interrupts off for eight milliseconds and
  became the longest region in the boot by a factor of fifteen. Eight is
  still hundreds of ticks, which is resolution enough, and core 0's
  longest region is back where it was.
- *And nothing is asserted about the frame count, which the first
  version of this stage did.* The count is the whole machine's and the
  other core is running, so an assertion that it is exactly what it was
  is an assertion that nothing else moved a frame in the instant this
  looked. M13 stage four ruled that out and M19 stage one's review had
  already taken the same assertion out of the flush check; this stage
  put it straight back in. What catches a leak is the boot's own frame
  ledger, which accounts for every frame still held when the run is
  over.
- *And the boot's flush count moved from seven to ten*, because the
  check's own invalidations are maintenance the other core has to hear
  about. That is the check paying for itself in the number it is
  measured against, and it is reported rather than hidden.

**7. What it cost, and sections 13.3, 15 and 18 written around it.**
*Built.*

- *Check.* The figures as counts: flushes removed, invalidations added,
  identifiers assigned and recycled in a boot, and the switch count that
  no longer flushes.
- Section 13.3 gains what a dispatch into another address space costs
  now. Section 15 gains the identifier, what is global and why, and the
  rule for reuse. Section 18's case is restated against a measurement
  rather than against a mechanism nobody had built, which is what
  section 9.2 asked for and could not have.

**What it settled.** Two lines in the compared part of the resource
report, so the counts are a diff against a file rather than a claim in
prose: `names: 2531 given out, 2499 again, 1 spaces without, 9 live`
and `names given back: 2522, each throwing away what was filed under
it`. Identical paced and burst on both ports, which is why they can be
compared at all.

**Two of the stage's four figures could not go below the line, and the
reasons are different.** The switch count moves with the host, for the
reason M6's review gave: it depends on when console input arrives, and
the same kernel gives 5472 burst against 5476 paced. The count of
switches that flushed does not move in either mode, but it differs by
port, ten on riscv64 and none on aarch64, and there is one compared
file for both tiers rather than one per configuration. Both are already
printed and asserted above the line, beside each other, where what is
checked is the relation between them rather than either number. The
other two counts the buffer path already reports, invalidations and
flushes, are on its own line and are not repeated.

**Falsified twice.** Raising `SYS_ASID_LIMIT` from 32 to 64 moved the
compared line from 2531 given out to 2563 and the diff failed. Removing
the `md_tlb_invalidate_asid()` call from the release path did not reach
the report at all: stage 4's own assertion caught it first, with `panic:
names: 0 identifiers thrown away when one space died`. That is the
right order for the two checks to fire in.

**And section 18 could not be restated against a saving.** Section 9.2
said identifiers would remove all 37 of M6's whole-TLB flushes and that
the case for a cohort therefore rests on forwarding rather than on
mapping. The flushes are gone by count, 10 of about 5470 on riscv64 and
0 on aarch64 against every one of them before. What is not available is
the saving, because QEMU discards every translation whenever the root
register is written, tagged or not. So section 18.5 says the case is
where M6 left it, undecided on mapping, and records that the mechanism
it was waiting on now exists. Section 18.5 also corrects M6's other
prediction: two narrow invalidations do cost about twice one, 20262 to
20562 ns against 10212 to 10325 on riscv64, but the kernel makes one,
and the reason it can is that neither call is narrow on this emulator
rather than anything about the design.

Section 13.3 gains what M12 could not see from inside the region: the
switch is four to seven microseconds and the refetch after it, for a
program touching 256 pages, is over a hundred. Section 15.7 is new and
says what the name is, that it is global and why, that it is
invalidated on release rather than on assignment, and that exhaustion
costs performance and not correctness. Section 15.6's paragraph about a
count of address spaces destroyed is corrected, because M19 stage two
removed that count and the name replaces it.

**What the review found.** Five things, four of them numbers written
from one sample each.

The switch count was quoted as 5476 or 5482, which was measured before
this stage changed the kernel. It is now 5472 burst and 5476 paced,
each stable across the runs taken. The count of switches that flushed
was quoted correctly at ten, but the comment beside the assertion that
checks it still said seven, from M19 stage five.

Every duration in sections 13.3 and 18.5 was one sample. Four runs of
each port give a spread the single numbers did not admit: a whole-TLB
flush is 11900 to 12600 ns on riscv64 and 14800 to 16300 on aarch64, a
page the walk wants back is 478 to 498 and 415 to 440, one broad
invalidation is 10275 to 10462 and 1484 to 2898, and one naming a space
is 10212 to 10325 and 2890 to 3056. All of them are now ranges with the
number of runs stated.

One of those ranges changed a claim. Section 18.5 said a call naming a
space costs what a broad call costs. On riscv64 the two overlap. On
aarch64 the named call is the dearer in all four runs, and the broad
call's own spread is wider than the gap between them, so the honest
statement is that the difference is not resolvable rather than that
there is none.

The exhaustion figure was read wrong. The check reports 27 built and 1
without, and 27 counts the one that went without, so it is the 27th
that runs unnamed and not the 28th: 6 names were in use of 32, 26 were
left, and building 27 spaces takes them all.

And the claim that the ten flushes are the cross-core case was true and
unargued. A switch also flushes into a space with no name, and the boot
builds such spaces, so the riscv64 count alone does not separate the
two causes. aarch64 builds the same spaces and reports zero, and the
only thing that differs between the ports is whether a fence reaches
the other core. That argument is now in section 13.3.

**Still untested.** The two compared lines assume a port with
identifiers. On a port reporting none, every space would go without a
name and the counts would be zero, zero, one per space, zero, and the
diff would fail for a reason that is not a defect. Both ports report 16
bits, so nothing here exercises it, and the shape of the compared file
is one per tier rather than one per configuration.

*Done when* a boot's address space switches keep their translations on
both ports and at Tier 2, a space that reuses an identifier sees its own
pages and not the previous holder's, and the cost of a flush and of the
maintenance that replaces it are both numbers rather than assertions.

*Would falsify.* That address space identifiers are the cheaper way to
buy what a cohort buys. If the bookkeeping to be correct about reuse
costs more than the flushes it removes, or if a port's identifier space
is too small to be worth managing, then the flush is the honest thing
and section 18's case is stronger than M6 left it. The measurement that
settles it is stage one's cost of a flush against stage six's cost of
the maintenance, in the same units on the same host.

*Watch for.* A check that cannot fail on the thing it is for, which this
project has produced in six consecutive milestones. Here the shape is
obvious in advance: a system with stale translations mostly works, and a
check that boots and prints has not tested tagging at all. Every stage's
check has to read a page whose content says which space it came from.
And a number that moves on its own: the switch count is not
deterministic, which M6's review found the hard way, so what is compared
has to be the flushes on that path and not how many times it was taken.

*Size.* Medium. Two ports, one field, and one mechanism for reuse, which
is the part that is neither small nor optional. The measurement either
side of it is most of the work and the reason to do it in this order.

---

### M20. The Pool Nothing Gives Back

**A channel is allocated once and lives until the machine stops.**

**Done.** All seven stages are built. Section 23 says what it
answered, what it cost, what the building kept finding, and what it
left untested. The gap it closed was in the kernel and half of one in
the specification: section 8 was incomplete rather than wrong, and
section 12 had never said what ends a channel.

A boot now makes 612 channels on a pool of 48 and gives 589 of them
back. The high-water mark fell from 40 to 24, used ends below it for
the first time in this system's life, and a server is restarted 52
times on one slot. The counting costs nothing measurable on the
rendezvous path: 888 ticks for the best round trip before the last
wrapper went in and 875 after.

Every other pool in this system returns what it lends. A process goes
back at its reap, a thread with it, a connection when its last
reference goes, a prepared program when its handle closes, a timer when
it is cancelled. `pool_free` is called for five object types. It is
never called for a channel.

The boot prints what that costs, and the shape of the number is the
argument: **40 channels used and 40 at once, of 48.** Used equals
high-water, which is true of no other pool here. Threads peak at 24 of
32 and end at fewer, connections at 12 of 32 and end at 7. A pool where
those two numbers are equal is not a pool being used carefully; it is a
pool nothing has ever given anything back to.

**This has already been paid for twice.** M17's review found the boot
at the end of its channels: at 32 slots the cohort check panicked with
"no channel" because checks earlier in the boot had spent them all, and
a check failed for something an unrelated check further up had done.
`SYS_MAX_CHANNELS` was raised to 48 and the reason was written where
the number is, along with the sentence this milestone exists to act on:
"the limit is not what is really short; what is short is that nothing
gives a channel back."

**And section 8 is the section it makes false.** Section 8 buys one
property: kernel memory consumption is a property of the configuration
rather than of the workload, so a system's footprint can be computed
from its build settings and cannot be driven upward by application
behaviour. For channels that is not true in the way that matters. The
footprint depends on how many channels the system has *ever* had, not
on how many it has, so a long-running system exhausts the pool at a
rate set by its history. No configuration fixes that; it only moves the
date. Section 8 also says a system that exhausts a pool must be
reconfigured and rebuilt, which is a reasonable thing to ask of a
concurrency bound and not of a counter.

**The reason it was never done is worth stating, because it is not
laziness.** A prepared program is its handle, so `prepared_free` at
release is correct by inspection. A channel is named by many handles,
by the connections opened over it, by every thread blocked sending on
it, by the pulse queue's contents, and by whatever the kernel itself
holds: a pager's channel, a cohort's, a namespace's. Freeing one means
knowing that none of those exist, and this kernel has never had to
know. What makes it tractable now is that M18 built connection
reference counting and M13 built the reap, so the two hardest holders
already say when they let go.

*Needs.* Nothing missing. The handle table already calls into
`kern_objref.c` on every retain and release, which is where four other
object types already learn that a handle came or went, and the pool
already has `pool_free` and generation counters that make a stale
reference say so rather than reach a stranger.

**What this is not.** Not a general garbage collector, and not a
reference count on every object type: the four that need one have one,
and this adds the fifth because it is measurably short. Not a change to
what a channel is or who owns it, which section 12.5 settled and M18
confirmed. Not dynamic allocation: the pool stays a build-time bound,
and what changes is whether a slot in it can be used twice.

**1. What is spent, and what of it is reachable.** *Built.*

- *Check.* The boot reports the channel pool the way it reports every
  other one, and adds the number nothing has ever printed: how many
  channels in use are named by no handle in any process's table and
  held by nothing in the kernel. That count is asserted to be greater
  than zero, because if it is zero the milestone has no subject and
  should be abandoned rather than built.
- Also asserted: used equals high-water, which is the mechanical
  statement of the same fact and the thing a later stage makes false.
  Both go in the compared report, at both tiers, since neither depends
  on when console input arrives.

**What it settled.** The milestone has a subject and the number is
worse than the pool size suggested. One line in the compared report at
each tier:

```
  channels: 40 in use, 40 at once, of 48, and 17 unreachable
  channels: 38 in use, 38 at once, of 48, and 16 unreachable
```

Tier 2 first, tier 0 second, and the same on both ports. **Nearly half
of what a boot spends on channels is already unreachable when the boot
ends.** Not held by a program that has stopped using them, not waiting
on anything: no handle in any process names them, no connection was
minted on them, no thread is inside or queued on them. Nothing in the
system can name them again and the slots are gone until the machine
stops.

**Four kinds of holder, which is the list stage two has to turn into a
count.** A handle in some process's table, which is the authority of
section 7 and the only one a program has. A connection minted on the
channel, per section 12.1, which is how a pager holds the channel a
process faults to. A thread inside a request on it, `t_serve_ch`,
which is section 12.3's link from a queued sender to whoever is
serving it. And a thread queued on it, receiving on it, or serving
from it, which the channel holds rather than the other way round but
which is still somebody standing on the floor.

**What the scan cannot see is the answer rather than a limitation of
it.** The boot holds channels in file-scope variables in `init_main.c`,
and those are counted as unreachable because that is exactly what they
are: a check made a channel, closed every handle to it, and no path in
this system will ever put the slot back. A scan that excused them
would be excusing the leak.

**Both numbers are asserted as well as compared**, which is unusual
and is deliberate in two ways. The compared file covers the paced run
and the burst run is only read for a panic, so a number this milestone
turns on should fail in both. And both assertions assert that a defect
is present: if nothing is ever unreachable the milestone has no
subject, and stage three is what makes the second one false.


**What the review found.** The scan read four structures that a
running program changes, with nothing to stop it changing them. Ten
processes are still running when the report is printed, and a handle
table being edited on the other core while this walked it would give a
count that no change caused, which is the one kind of number this
project will not put in a compared file. The walk now takes the kernel
lock and turns interrupts off, and reads the pool's own used and
high-water inside the same region, so all four numbers on the line
come from one moment rather than three.

**And that region is 636 to 760 microseconds, which is the price and
is worth stating.** Core 0's longest region in the same boot is about
1030 microseconds and a console line is about the same, so the scan is
the second longest thing in the boot that holds interrupts off. It is
not the lock: taking it out changed the figure by less than the spread
between runs, and Tier 0, where the lock does not exist and there is
one core, measures the same. It is about 800 iterations at this
emulator's speed, which is the usual right shape and wrong magnitude.

**The region is not measured by the instrument that measures regions.**
Section 13.3's report is printed a few lines above this, so a region
opened afterwards cannot appear in it. Moving the scan earlier would
make it visible and would then very likely replace the kernel's own
longest region in a figure that is supposed to be about the kernel.
Printing the duration is what stands in for being measured, and the
number above says what it would have been.

**An obvious saving was available and was not taken.** A handle table
has room for 64 and a process holds a handful, so the walk could stop
once the table's own count is accounted for. Measured, it saved
nothing, and it would turn a table whose count had drifted from its
slots into a scan that quietly stopped short. The full walk stays and
the drift is now a panic instead: `a table says %u handles and holds
%u`.

**The index a holder names is checked rather than assumed.** Every
pointer marked comes out of a structure the walk is reading, and one
being changed underneath could hand back something that is not a
channel. An index past the end of the array would have been a write
past the end of the caller's stack.

**Falsified four ways.** Dropping the connection walk from the scan
moved the compared line from 17 unreachable to 18 and the diff failed,
which also says the pager's channel is held by nothing else. Making
the scan mark every slot fired `channels: nothing is unreachable, so
there is nothing here to give back`. Allocating and freeing one slot
before the scan fired `channels: 40 in use against 41 at once, so
something already gives one back`. Adding one to the count of handles
found fired `channels: a table says 34 handles and holds 35`.

**Found and not this stage's:** the `connections:` line in the tier 0
compared report says 7 in use paced and 8 in use burst. `make check`
diffs the paced run and only greps the burst one, so a number that
moves between the two modes sits in a compared file unnoticed. It is
M18's line rather than this milestone's, and it is exactly what M6's
review ruled against. The channels line was checked against the same
hazard in all eight combinations of port, tier and mode and does not
move; the count of handle tables does, which is why it is above the
line and not in the file.

**2. A channel knows what holds it.** *Built.*

- *Check.* A count on the channel, maintained where the other four
  object types are, and a scan that walks every handle table in the
  system and every kernel-side holder and arrives at the same number
  for every channel. The scan is the check and it runs at several
  points in the boot, not only at the end.
- The scan is expected to disagree the first time it is run, and where
  it disagrees is the deliverable of this stage: the holders nobody had
  written down. Nothing is freed yet.

**What it settled.** `c_holds` counts two things and not four: one for
every handle in any process's table that names the channel, whatever
its rights, and one for every connection minted on it. The walk agrees
with it at four points in the boot, and the number of channels holding
nothing that the count produces is the same 17 and 16 that stage one's
independent definition produced.

**Four holders turned out to be three.** Stage one listed a thread
inside a request as a holder separately from the channel's own serving
list. They are the same fact: `serving_begin` sets `t_serve_ch` and
links the thread onto `c_serving` in one place, so counting both
double-counts, which is what the walk said the first time it ran
against the new count. The thread lists are therefore tested on the
channel rather than counted into `c_holds`: a count is for what is
somewhere else, and a list head is cheaper to test than to keep a
number for. The two sides are still required to agree, which is the
only check there has ever been that the pair stays a pair.

**And the walk found something nobody was looking for: the console
channel's serving list does not end.** Section 19.3 says a server
thread serves one request at a time and nothing enforces it, which the
README has listed as a limitation since M16, described as leaving a
list "naming a thread that is serving nothing". What it actually does,
when the second request arrives on the *same* channel the thread is
already serving, is read the thread out of `c_serving` and write it
back as its own successor. The list becomes a ring. The console driver
does this in every paced session, when a line is typed at it, and
nothing in this kernel had ever walked that list to the end, so
nothing had noticed.

The fix is that `serving_begin` does nothing when the thread is
already serving that channel. The thread is already recorded as being
inside a request there, which is what the list is for, and recording
it twice was never going to tell a walker anything. Refusing the
second request is section 19.3's business and is not done here.

**The walks are bounded now, and that was learned the hard way.** The
first version of this check walked the lists to their end, and on a
paced session it did not come back: the boot printed everything up to
the interrupt-to-a-program report and then stopped, and a run left for
four hundred seconds printed nothing more. A diagnostic that hangs the
machine is worse than one that says what it found, so a walk that
passes more threads than the machine has now panics with which list it
was on.

**A correction to stage one's review.** That review reported the walk
as costing 636 to 760 microseconds and attributed it to "about 800
iterations at this emulator's speed". It is not. The walk now runs
five times in a boot, and the first costs 700 to 1090 microseconds
while every later one costs 43 to 71. The difference is QEMU
translating the code before it can run it, paid once. The walk itself
is about 50 microseconds, which also means the region it holds the
kernel for is a twentieth of the longest region in the boot rather
than two thirds of it. Both figures are printed.

**Falsified four ways.** Dropping the count when a handle closes fired
`channel half: the kernel says 2 hold it and 1 do`. Not counting a
connection fired `channel fs: let go of more often than held`, from
the other side and earlier than the walk. Putting the self-link back
fired `channel console: its serving list passes 32 threads and does
not end`. Removing one of the walk sites fired `channels: 3 walks, not
4`.

**What did not happen.** The cross-channel case of the same
limitation, where a thread serving one channel takes a request on
another, does not occur in this boot: the count of serving entries
left behind is zero in all eight combinations of port, tier and mode.
It is worth saying that it would be worse than the README describes if
it did. `t_serve_next` is one field shared by every serving list, so a
thread that moves to another channel's list overwrites the link that
belonged to the first, and the first list runs into the second rather
than merely holding a stale name.

**3. The last holder frees the slot.** *Built.*

- *Check.* A channel created and dropped leaves the pool with the same
  number of slots in use it started with, and the slot that comes back
  is the same slot, which the generation counter says. Used falls below
  high-water for the first time in this system's life, so stage one's
  second assertion has to be rewritten and the compared report changes.
- Falsifiable by removing the free: used equals high-water again and
  the diff fails.

**What it settled.** The compared line, at Tier 2 and Tier 0:

```
  channels: 24 in use, 25 at once, of 48, 18 given back, 1 nothing names
  channels: 23 in use, 24 at once, of 48, 17 given back, 1 nothing names
```

Against `40 in use, 40 at once` two stages ago. **The high-water mark
fell from 40 to 25**, which is the number that matters: it is what the
pool would have to be sized for, and it went down by nearly half
without anything in the boot doing less. Seventeen or eighteen slots
come back in a boot, and used is below high-water for the first time
in this system's life, which is the sentence every other pool here
could already say.

**The slot's identity is checked and not only the count.** A pool
handing out a fresh slot every time while freeing old ones would
report the same thing until it ran out. So one channel is made, its
index and generation noted, its only handle closed, and another made:
the same index, the generation moved from 5 to 6, and the pool exactly
where it started. The freed channel's identifier finds nothing, which
is section 7.1's rule and the reason a slot can be reused at all.

**Stage one's two assertions are turned over rather than deleted.**
They asserted that nothing was reachable and that nothing was ever
given back, and said at the time that stage three was what would make
them false. What is asserted now is that slots come back and that the
pool holds fewer than it has had out at once. A third assertion is new
and is the one with teeth: no slot may be sitting there with nothing
naming it, nobody inside it and no pulse waiting. Since the free
happens when the last holder lets go, a slot in that state got there
afterwards, and the day that happens is the day something has to look
again.

**Four things stop a free, and one of them stops one every boot.** A
thread queued to send, a thread blocked receiving, a thread inside a
request, and a pulse nobody has collected. A channel that reaches zero
holders while any of those is true is not freed, and nothing tries
again, which is a leak in the safe direction. It is counted rather
than argued about: one slot a boot, and the report names it. It is
`hints`, which has an uncollected pulse, and it is stage four's to
deal with.

**Falsified three ways.** Removing the free fired `channels: 24 in use
after the one made here went, not 23`, from the identity check rather
than the report. Freeing without asking whether anyone was inside
changed the compared line to `19 given back, 0 nothing names` and the
diff failed; worth noting that nothing else caught it, so the pulse
that was thrown away was thrown away silently, which is stage four's
subject. Freeing only the even-numbered slots fired `channels: 5 slots
are free in every sense and still held`.

**What the boot's own pointers did.** Freeing a channel whose handles
have all closed makes the boot's file-scope pointers to it dangle,
which was the risk in doing this at all, and nothing in the boot
touches one afterwards. The name and owner are cleared before the slot
goes back, so a pointer somebody kept reads as an unnamed channel
rather than as the one that used to be there. The generation is what
makes a handle safe; nothing makes a raw pointer safe.

**What the review found.** The free tested the three lists and the
pulse count with interrupts off and nothing else, and then gave the
slot back. Interrupts off says nothing about the other core. Every one
of the eighteen frees in this boot happens on a kernel thread, which
never entered the kernel and so holds none of its exclusion, so the
other core could have been inside a rendezvous putting a thread on one
of the lists being tested. The test and the free now happen under the
kernel lock, and so does stage one's walk.

**Taken only if this core does not already hold it.** A call arriving
from a vector already has the lock and taking it twice is refused
rather than deadlocked, so the question has to be asked; `klock_held`
is no longer private to `kern_lock.c`. How often that matters is now
printed, and the answer in this boot is never: **0 of 18 slots go back
from inside a system call.** The branch exists for the path that will
exist and nothing here exercises it.

**A hazard was looked for and is not there.** Five fields of `struct
channel` were never written at creation, and M18's own comment
predicted that this would matter the day a slot came back, which is
this stage. It does not. `pool_alloc` clears every object it hands
out, every time and not only the first, so a recycled slot arrives as
zero exactly as a fresh one does. The field that would have been felt
is `c_pulse_lost`: a channel can be freed with it set, and the next
occupant would have told its server it had missed something that
happened before it existed.

The five fields are written now anyway, so that a reader of
`channel_create` can see what a channel starts as without knowing what
the pool does with the memory first, and a check on the reused slot
asserts it comes back with no pulses, no lost flag and no lists. That
check could not be falsified: taking the clear out of `pool_alloc`
stops the boot at the clock check, several thousand lines of output
before this. It is a guard against a future change to the pool rather
than a test of anything this stage built, and it is worth having on
those terms.

**4. What must not be freed under somebody.** *Built.*

- *Check.* Four constructions, each dropping every handle and asserting
  the slot is still in use and the party still correct, then releasing
  the party and asserting the slot comes back: a thread blocked sending
  on it, an undelivered pulse in its queue, a live connection over it,
  and a cohort member's outstanding rendezvous.
- Each is falsifiable by freeing early rather than by an argument: the
  check then reads a channel that has been handed to somebody else, and
  the generation says stale where it should say the object.

**What it settled.** Of the four things proposed, three are parties
and one is not.

```
  with a sender queued on it             kept
  with a server inside a request         kept
  with a thread blocked receiving        kept
  with a connection over it              kept
  with a pulse nobody can collect        given back, and the pulse with it
```

Each is built, every handle is closed under it, the slot is required
to still be there, and then the party is let out and the slot is
required to come back. Asserting only the second half would pass on a
kernel that freed the channel at once and got away with it, which is
the shape of every check this project has had to throw away.

**A pulse is not somebody.** Stage three treated an uncollected pulse
as a reason to keep the slot, and left one channel a boot in that
state for it. A pulse is collected by receiving on the channel,
receiving needs a handle, and by the time this question is asked there
are none: nothing that exists or can come to exist will ever collect
it. Keeping the slot was keeping it for a message with no possible
reader. The pulses go with the channel and the count of them is in the
compared report, eight in a boot.

**And the free had to learn to try again.** Stage three freed a
channel only at the moment the last holder let go, so a channel a
thread was inside was never looked at again. The three operations
that let a thread out of a channel now ask: a receive, which takes a
sender off the queue and this thread off the receivers, and a reply,
which takes this thread off the serving list. Both are wrapped rather
than having the question asked at each of their returns, of which
there are five and three. The channel a reply is on has to be read
before the reply, because after it this thread is serving nothing.

**The cohort member's rendezvous is the serving case and adds nothing
to it.** What keeps the slot is an entry on the serving list, and a
cohort member inside a request puts exactly that there. The check is
built with a kernel thread instead, because the obstacle is what is
being tested and a cohort would only make the construction longer.

**The numbers moved again.** 23 in use against 24 at once at Tier 2,
from 24 and 25, with 23 slots given back in a boot against 18. The
high-water mark is 24, having been 40 three stages ago.


**What the review found.** Both wrappers kept the channel as a
pointer across an operation that blocks. A receive puts the lock down
across a switch, and a reply hands the core to the client it woke, so
by the time either comes back something else can have taken the last
hold and freed the slot. Reading `c_holds` through the old pointer
would then read whatever occupies the slot now, and finding zero
there would free a channel somebody is using. Both keep the
identifier instead and look it up again: the generation says the slot
has moved on, and the lookup returns nothing rather than the wrong
thing. Nothing in this boot exercises the window, in the same way
nothing exercises stage three's lock guard.

**And the pulses that go are not all the same kind.** Eight go with a
channel in a boot and one of them is reserved: section 13.1's kind,
and specifically `SYS_PULSE_PEER_GONE` on `hints`. That is the one
M18 built and then deliberately made losable, because the fact it
carries moved onto the connection and the pulse became a hint. So
discarding it costs a server a prompt wakeup it was never going to
get, since the server is what has gone. The compared report says both
numbers rather than the total, because a reserved pulse quietly
becoming common is the thing worth noticing.

**A residue the assertion does not cover.** A connection kept for
reaping, per M18 stage four, holds its channel, so a channel whose
server has died with uncollected connections on it is held by them
and nothing will ever collect. The end-of-boot assertions do not see
it: holds is above zero, so it is reachable by the walk's definition
and counts as neither free nor stuck. It shows only as a slot still
in use, which the compared line pins. Stage five is the case that
would produce it on purpose.

**Falsified six ways**, one per obstacle, one for the retry, one for
the kinds. Ignoring the sender queue fired `the slot went with a
sender queued on it`; ignoring the receivers, `the slot went with a
thread receiving`; ignoring the serving list, `the slot went with a
server inside it`; keeping the slot for a pulse again, `the slot
stayed for a pulse nobody can collect`; removing the retry, `the slot
stayed after everybody left`; and counting every discarded pulse as
reserved moved the compared line from 1 to 8.

**5. A server that restarts under its clients.** *Built.*

- *Check.* The case sections 18.2 and 18.3 argue from and which nothing
  in this system has ever done, and M18's retrospective named it as
  untested. A supervisor kills a server, the channels the server owned
  come back, and it launches a replacement that makes its own. After
  more restarts than the pool has slots, the pool is where it started.
- What this settles beyond the count is whether a client holding a send
  handle across the restart is told the right thing, which is the
  difference section 12.5 draws between `SYS_ERR_STALE` and
  `SYS_ERR_OWNER_DEAD`, and which no client here has ever acted on.

**What it settled.** Fifty-two servers started and ended, four more
than the pool has slots, **every one of them on the same slot**, and
the pool exactly where it began with its high-water mark unmoved. M16
built the other half of this: a server killed and replaced with the
kernel holding the channel across the gap and handing a duplicate to
each one, which is a restart where the channel never goes. Here the
server is given the only handle there is, so the channel is its own in
the sense section 12.5 means, and it goes when the server does.

**The channel comes back at the reap and not at the exit.** A join
says the process has ended; its handle table closes when the last
thing that can ask about it lets go, and the collection happens at the
top of some core's next switch. That is section 15.6's own
distinction, and the check waits rather than assuming.

**And a client holding a connection across the end is told nothing.**
That is not the answer the stage went looking for and it is the right
one. The channel is kept, because a connection is a holder and a
client with something to send on is a reason for the object to exist.
The send then queues, and what gets the client back is its own
deadline: twenty milliseconds later, `SYS_ERR_TIMEOUT`, with the clock
saying it waited the whole of it.

Section 12.5's two errors say what a client is told when the server it
was **already talking to** went. A client that starts talking
afterwards is a different question and the kernel cannot answer it: a
channel whose owner is gone is exactly what a channel looks like
between a server being killed and its replacement taking the receive
right, which is the restart M16 built and made invisible to clients on
purpose. Refusing the send would make every restart visible to every
client. So the two cases differ and neither is the kernel knowing
which happened.

**A kill that is accepted and does nothing.** Killing a server whose
thread is ready and has never run leaves it alive. The mark is set,
`thread_cancel` finds nothing blocked to release, and the thread then
runs, enters user mode and blocks in a receive that never asks whether
its process is dying. Measured: the thread goes from `THREAD_READY` to
`THREAD_BLOCKED` on `THREAD_WAIT_RECV` with `p_exited` still false,
and the join waits out thirty seconds and then six hundred. The
comment in `proc_kill` states the assumption that fails, that a ready
thread "has already stopped somewhere in this kernel, and it finds the
mark on the way back out". A thread that has never run has not
stopped anywhere, and nothing on the path to blocking looks at the
mark.

This is section 10.5's promptness not being kept, it is not this
milestone's to fix, and the check waits for the server to reach its
receive point rather than working around it silently. A supervisor
would wait for the same thing.

**Falsified three ways.** Keeping a handle in the kernel across the
restart fired `restarts: 2 hold a channel the server owns`. Making a
connection stop holding its channel fired stage two's walk first,
`channel fs: the kernel says 1 hold it and 2 do`, which is the right
order for those two checks. Freeing a channel one connection still
holds fired `channels: slot 3 is free and 1 things name it`.

**And two counts elsewhere moved.** `kills` went from 15 to 68 and the
queued half of `deadlines` from 1 to 2, both because this stage kills
fifty-three servers and leaves one client to time out. Both are in the
compared report and both were updated with the reason written where
the number is.

**What the review found: the stage had no clients.** The title says a
server that restarts under its clients, and the fifty-two rounds did
not have one. Each round made the channel, gave it to a server, killed
the server and waited for the slot. Nothing ever sent on it, so what
was being measured was a server that restarts, which M16 already
built. Each round now keeps a send handle of its own across the kill,
sends a request and requires a reply before killing, and asserts that
exactly one thing holds the channel at the moment the kill goes in.
Fifty-two requests are served, which is asserted rather than reported,
and a round where the server never ran would now be caught by the
missing reply rather than by the count of slots at the end.

That also removes the wait for the server to reach its receive point,
which was working around the kill defect above by guessing at timing.
A reply is proof the server ran, and it is a fact rather than a guess.

**A read through a pointer that the check is about.** The loop that
held a client across the restart read `channel_holds` through the
channel pointer it had kept. If the slot had gone and been reused,
that reads the new occupant's count and says the check passed. It is
exactly the case the stage exists to detect, read in the way that
cannot detect it. The loop keeps the identifier and looks it up each
round; a lookup that returns nothing panics with `restarts: the
channel went under a live client`.

**Two spin loops with no bound.** Stage four waited for a sender to
queue and for a receiver to arrive by yielding until the list was
non-empty, which on a kernel that never puts them there is a paced
session that stops printing, the same failure stage two spent a boot
diagnosing. Both wait a second and then panic with what never
happened.

**Falsified once more.** Leaving the client's handle open across the
kill fired `restarts: 2 hold a channel the server owns`, which is the
new assertion catching from the client's side what the earlier
falsification caught from the kernel's.

**6. More channels than the pool has.** *Built.*

- *Check.* M13's shape, which is the one that actually proves reuse: a
  path that spends channels, run more times than there are slots, with
  the total and the pool size printed beside each other. It completes,
  and the high-water mark does not move after the first cycle.
- Falsifiable by the pool running out, which is what happens today
  after 48 of them.

**What it settled.** **Five hundred and twelve channels were made and
ended on a pool of forty-eight**, sixty-four cycles of eight alive
together, and the pool came back to where it started after every one
of them.

```
    channels made and ended                512, of 48 slots
    spent in                               64 cycles, 8 alive at a time
    the high-water mark                    21, from the first cycle on
    slots in use after all of it           13, where it started
    what the whole of it took              about 51086 us, 99 us a channel
```

Stage five already spent fifty-two, one at a time, which says a slot
comes back. It does not say the pool can carry a load. One slot going
round is the easiest case there is, and a kernel that leaked a slot
for every two it freed would pass it. Eight at once and sixty-four
times is the case that separates them.

**The mark is set by the first cycle and nothing after it moves it.**
Twenty at Tier 0 and twenty-one at Tier 2, from a pool sitting at
twelve or thirteen when the check starts. That is the assertion M13's
loop is built around, and it fails for a kernel that hands out a fresh
slot each time while freeing the old ones as surely as for one that
leaks.

**And it cost the boot's own figure nothing.** The compared line still
says `23 in use, 24 at once` at Tier 2, unchanged by five hundred and
twelve channels, because the check's peak of twenty-one is below what
the shell reaches later anyway. What moved is the count given back, 76
to 588, which is the whole of what this stage adds to the report.

**The same slots every cycle, and never the same generation.** The
eight slots a cycle takes are sorted and compared against the eight
the first cycle took: the same set, sixty-three times over. Each one's
generation has to be strictly greater than the last time that slot was
seen, which is what says the slot was genuinely handed back rather
than never given up. Stage three checks this for one channel; this is
the same rule under load, where a pool with an off-by-one in its free
list would show it.

**Both orders out.** A channel here is held by a handle and by a
connection, and which one lets go last decides which path through the
free runs. Half the channels in a cycle close the receive handle
first, leaving the connection holding the slot, and half close the
send handle first, leaving the handle holding it. After the first
close the slot is required to still be there, and after the second to
be gone. Asserting only the second half would pass on a kernel that
freed the channel at the first close and got away with it.

**What a channel costs, reported and not asserted.** Between 72 and
105 microseconds for a create, a handle, a connection and two closes,
across both ports, both tiers and both modes; 37 to 63 milliseconds
for the whole check. That is the host's figure and it is above no
compared line, per M9's rule. It is also why this check sits where it
does: sixty milliseconds does not move the shell, and M13's loop had
to be moved to the end of the boot for costing two seconds.

**Falsified five ways, and two of them never got here.** Removing the
free entirely fired stage four first, `holds: the slot stayed after
everybody left`, and refusing one free in sixteen fired stage four as
well, `holds: the slot stayed after the connection went`. That is the
right order and it is worth writing down: a leak big enough to matter
is caught by a check that makes four channels, long before a check
that makes five hundred sees it. To reach this stage at all, the
defect had to be scoped to the channels it spends.

Scoped that way, never freeing them fired `spent: the slot outlived
both its handles on cycle 0`; leaking one in sixteen of them fired the
same assertion on cycle 1. Putting a freed slot on the back of the
free list rather than the front, so that a fresh slot comes out each
time, fired `spent: cycle 1 took slot 21 where the first took 13`.
Taking two extra slots and giving them straight back at the peak of a
later cycle, which no per-slot assertion can see, fired `spent: the
mark went from 21 to 23 on cycle 2`.

**What the last of those says about the mark.** Every leak this stage
can see shows first in the count of slots in use, which is asserted
back to where it started after each cycle. The high-water assertion
earns its place on the one thing that assertion cannot see: a peak
reached inside a cycle and gone by the end of it.

**What the review found: an assertion that was arithmetic.** The loop
asserted that the number of channels it had spent equalled the number
of cycles times the number per cycle. The counter is incremented on
the line after the create, so it can only ever be what the loop bounds
say, and the assertion was checking that multiplication works. It is
replaced by the count the kernel keeps of slots given back, read
before and after and required to equal the number made. That is a
different number arrived at down a different path, and 512 out means
512 back.

Falsified by not counting one free in a hundred: `spent: 512 channels
made and 507 slots given back`. Nothing else in the boot notices,
because the slots really do come back; what is wrong is the number the
compared report prints.

**A duplicate the comparison could not see.** The eight slots a cycle
takes are compared against the first cycle's eight, which catches a
pool that hands out the wrong slots. It does not catch a pool that
hands out the same slot twice, because a set with a duplicate in it on
the first cycle is the set every later cycle is measured against. The
sorted slots are now required to be distinct, which is the worst
failure this pool could have and was the one thing the check assumed.

Falsified by handing one channel slot out twice without taking it off
the free list: `spent: slot 16 came out twice on cycle 2`. Doing the
same to whichever pool happened to be next, which turned out to be the
connection pool, fired `spent: the slot outlived both its handles on
cycle 1` instead, from the hold that was then released once too few.

**Every slot saw one order and only one.** The two close orders
alternated on the position in the cycle, and the slots come back in a
fixed order, so slot X closed handle-first on all sixty-four cycles
and slot Y connection-first on all sixty-four. Half the coverage the
comment claimed. The order now turns on the cycle as well as the
position.

**And the report printed the wrong variable.** The line reading slots
in use after all of it printed the value read before the loop. It was
true, because the assertion after every cycle makes it true, but a
report line that prints an assumption rather than a reading says
nothing. It reads the pool.

**7. What it cost, and sections 8 and 12 written around it.** *Built.*

- *Check.* The figures as counts: slots reclaimed in a boot, the
  high-water mark against the number spent, and the restart count from
  stage five.
