- Section 8's property is restated against what is now true of every
  pool rather than of four of five. Section 12 gains what a channel's
  lifetime is and what ends it, which the specification does not say
  anywhere today. If stage two finds a holder that cannot be counted,
  section 8 gains the exception instead, written as an exception.

**What it settled.** The compared report, at Tier 2 and Tier 0:

```
  channels: 611 made, 588 given back, 23 live
  channels at once: 24 of 48, and 52 restarts of a server on one slot
  channels: 609 made, 587 given back, 22 live
  channels at once: 23 of 48, and 52 restarts of a server on one slot
```

Four counts in place of the four this milestone started with. The
first line is the milestone in one sentence: **611 channels made, 588
given back, 23 still here.** The second puts the number spent against
the bound, which is the claim being made. The pool is 48 and nothing
ever held more than 24 of them.

**The shape of the line changed and that is the point.** Stage one
printed `40 in use, 40 at once, of 48`, which is what a pool is
normally asked. The interesting question about a channel is no longer
how many there are, it is how many have been and gone, so the number
made leads and the pool's own figures follow it. M19's two lines about
names are the precedent for the shape: given out, given out again,
live.

**One identity and two floors, asserted as well as compared.** Made
has to equal given back plus live, which ties three counters kept in
three different places to each other: a channel that was made either
went back or is still here. The number made has to exceed the pool
size, or the line is measuring nothing. And the restarts have to name
a slot the pool actually has.

**The count of creations is taken under a lock.** Two cores can be
making channels at once, and a counter that loses an increment is a
number in a compared file that moves on its own, which is the failure
M6's review named. It goes under the same lock the holds are counted
under.

**Section 8 gains the half it was missing.** It bought one property,
that kernel memory is a function of the configuration rather than of
the workload, and that property is worth nothing on its own: a pool
that never takes an object back has a fixed footprint and still stops
at a date set by its history. So the section now says what the size
of a pool bounds, which is how many objects exist at one time and not
how many may ever be made, and says the rule that makes it true for
every type. The channel is written in as the exception that was, with
what it cost and what it costs now.

**Section 12 gains 12.8, a channel's lifetime**, which the
specification never stated. Six things hold a channel and they are
listed. The slot goes back when the last of them lets go and nobody
is standing in it. An uncollected pulse is not a holder, and why. A
channel outliving its owner is normal, which is section 12.5 seen
from the object's side. And what the identifier guarantees against
what a raw pointer does not, which is the rule the kernel's own paths
had to learn in stage four.

**Falsified two ways, and the second is weaker than it looks.** Not
counting one create in a hundred fired `channels: 605 made against
588 back and 23 live`, which is the identity doing its job. Taking
stage six's loop out of the boot changed the compared line to `99
made, 76 given back, 23 live` and the diff failed, but the assertion
that the boot makes more channels than the pool holds did not fire:
99 is already more than 48. That assertion is a floor against the day
the boot stops exercising this at all, and the compared report is
what actually catches a check going missing. It is written here
rather than left to look stronger than it is.

**What the review found: writing 12.8 found a leak.** The section had
to say what ends a channel, and saying it meant listing the ways a
thread leaves one. There are three, the code's own comment says three,
and only two of them ask whether the slot can go. A receive asks and a
reply asks. **A send does not.** So a channel whose holders all went
while a thread was queued on it is given back when that thread is
served, and leaked when it gives up. A deadline, a cancellation, an
owner that died: on all of those the thread comes off the queue and
leaves the channel just as empty, and nothing was asking.

Stage four did not find it because its check released the sender by
receiving, which is the path that works. The check now builds the
other one: a sender queues, its only handle is closed under it, nobody
ever receives, and what gets it back is its own twenty millisecond
deadline. The slot has to be there while it waits and gone once it has
given up.

The send is wrapped the way the receive and the reply are, around the
whole operation rather than at each of its seven returns, and by
identifier rather than by pointer for the reason stage four's review
settled. Falsified by taking the wrapper's question out again:
`holds: the slot stayed after the sender gave up`.

**And it costs nothing measurable.** The wrapper is on every send,
which is the hottest path in the kernel. The best round trip in the
boot was 888 ticks, about 88 microseconds, before this and 875 ticks,
about 87 microseconds, after. That is a question worth asking of any
change to that path and the answer here is no.

**Section 12.8 said the wrong thing about who holds a channel.** It
listed six holders, put connections among the things read from lists
when they are counted, and named the kernel's own references as a
sixth. That last one is false and it is false in the direction that
matters: a bare `struct channel *` holds nothing, prevents nothing,
and the pointers the boot keeps are exactly what stage three found
dangling. What keeps a pager's channel alive is the handle the kernel
holds, not the pointer it reaches it through. The section now says two
holders and three things that stand in it, and says plainly that a
kernel pointer is neither.

**Three numbers read at three moments, asserted to be an identity.**
Made, given back and live were read from three places at three
different times and required to add up. The scan already takes the
pool's own figures inside its locked region so that they describe one
moment; the two counters go in there with them. The identity is now a
statement about an instant.

**And a report line that said nothing when its check did not run.**
The restart count and slot were asserted only against the pool size,
and both default to zero, which is a slot the pool has. The count is
now required to be the number of rounds the loop runs. Falsified by
dropping the line that records it: `channels: 0 restarts in the
report, not 52`.

*Done when* a channel's slot comes back when nothing holds it, the boot
spends more channels than the pool has and does not run out, a server
can be restarted under its clients, and `SYS_MAX_CHANNELS` is a bound
on how many channels exist at once rather than on how many may ever be
made.

*Would falsify.* That a channel can be given back at all for what the
counting costs. If the holders cannot all be found, or if the count
needs a branch on a path that cannot afford one, then the honest answer
is that a channel lives as long as the system, `SYS_MAX_CHANNELS` is a
configuration number like any other, and section 8 gains a written
exception rather than a quiet one. The measurement that settles it is
stage two's scan against the count: if the scan and the count cannot be
made to agree, nothing after stage two is safe to build.

*Watch for.* A check that cannot fail, which is now seven consecutive
milestones. The shape here is specific and different from M19's: the
pool is small and the checks run in a boot that is already spending it,
so a check that makes a channel, drops it, and finds a free slot has
found the slot somebody else was not using. Every check has to assert
the identity of the slot it got back and not merely that there was one.
And a count that moves on its own: the channel count depends on what
the shell session opens, so what is compared has to be what the checks
spend and give back, measured between two readings, rather than the
pool's total.

*Size.* Medium. One count, one free, and four holders to find. The
holders are the part that is neither small nor known in advance, and
stage two exists to find out how bad it is before anything depends on
the answer.

---

### M21. The Kill a Thread Can Outlast

**A process killed before its first thread has run is not killed.**

**Done.** All seven stages are built. Section 24 says what it answered,
what it cost, what the building kept finding, and what it left
untested. The gap it closed was one path into user mode that nothing
checked the mark on, and it found that there are three such paths
rather than two.

A kill now reaches a thread that has never run: 54 threads a boot end
at a trampoline, 53 of them a program's first thread and one a thread a
program made, and a supervisor is told 365 to 509 microseconds after
asking, against never. A marked thread starts no operation, because the
mark is read before an entry rather than after it, which stops 22
threads a boot. One kill ends four threads in the four states a kill
has to reach. A thread is refused to a process that is over, whether it
was killed or ended on its own. And M20 stage five's restart loop kills
its servers without first asking them for anything.

The compared report holds the whole set and the doors out of it:

```
  threads a kill had to reach: 81, and all of them ended
  by one of three doors: 54 a trampoline, 22 an entry boundary, 4 a trap, 1 already leaving
```

Section 10.5 is written to it, and section 10.2 gained what happens to
a thread created in a process that is over.

`sys_proc_kill()` marks the process and cancels every thread of it, and
a thread that is not blocked has nothing to cancel. `proc_kill`'s own
comment states the assumption that carries the rest: a thread that is
ready "has already stopped somewhere in this kernel, and it finds the
mark on the way back out". That is true of a thread that was preempted
or released, because both return to user mode through a trap path that
reads the mark. It is false of a thread that has never run. There is no
trap to return from. `proc_user_start` and `proc_thread_start` drop
into user mode without looking at anything.

M20 stage five measured it. A server is spawned and killed at once: the
thread goes from `THREAD_READY` to `THREAD_BLOCKED` on
`THREAD_WAIT_RECV` with `p_exited` still false, the join waits out
thirty seconds and then ten minutes, and the supervisor is told
`SYS_OK` for a kill that did nothing. The check had to send the server
a request and require a reply before killing it, which is a workaround
written into a check to get past a defect in the kernel.

**And the mark is read after an entry rather than before one.** The
system call path checks `p_dying` at the end of each entry, which is
where M17 put it, and the comment there is about not running fifteen
more operations. The consequence nothing said is that an entry which
blocks is never followed by the check at all: the thread is inside the
operation, and the operation is a wait. So a marked thread that has
not yet run does not merely reach user mode, it reaches the first
blocking call it makes and stays there.

**Section 10.5 claims promptness and the claim is currently false.**
The section says process termination "promptly unblocks all threads of
the target process exactly as if each had been cancelled
individually". M17 wrote a subsection under it saying who a kill
reaches and what it costs, and that subsection is where the correction
belongs: it says a thread that is not blocked "has nothing to release,
and the mark is left for it to find", which assumes every way back to
user mode looks. Two do not.

**What makes this worth a milestone rather than a fix.** The same
sentence covers three different paths into user mode and only one of
them was ever checked against it. A supervisor is the party that
suffers, and supervision is what sections 18.2 and 18.3 are built on:
a cohort restart that kills a member and starts a replacement is
exactly the sequence that produces a never-run thread, and it is the
sequence M20 could not write without a workaround. The fix is small.
Finding out how many other ways into user mode exist, and proving
there are no more, is not.

*Needs.* Nothing missing. The mark, the kill code and
`proc_exit_if_dying` all exist; M17 built them and M20 measured where
they are not consulted.

**What this is not.** Not a change to what a kill means or to what a
supervisor is told, which section 10.5 settles. Not cancellation of a
thread that is computing, which M17 built with the poke and which
works. Not the reentrancy guard: a thread interrupted inside a kernel
operation is still not ended there, for the reason that has not
changed.

**1. What a kill does not reach, counted.** *Built.*


- *Check.* A process spawned and killed before its thread has run, and
  the boot reports what happened to it: whether the thread ended, what
  it ended with, and how long the supervisor waited. Asserted to be
  the wrong answer, because if it is the right one the milestone has
  no subject. The count goes in the compared report at both tiers.
- Also counted: entries a marked thread makes, which `p_dying_entries`
  already records and which M17 reports for one program. The number
  this stage adds is entries a marked thread *starts*, which is the
  one the after-the-entry check cannot see.
- Falsifiable by the case not reproducing, which would mean M20's
  measurement was of something else.

**What it settled.** The milestone has a subject and the shape of it
is exact. One line in the compared report at each tier:

```
  kills a thread outlasted: 1, entries started while marked: 1
```

A server is spawned and killed inside one deferral, so the kill is
written while its thread is `THREAD_READY` and has not been
dispatched. `sys_proc_kill()` returns `SYS_OK`, the mark is set, and
about 800 to 1000 microseconds later the thread is blocked in a
receive with the process not exited. It got there by being
dispatched, entering user mode, and making one system call, which the
kernel counted as an entry started by a marked thread and then ran to
completion anyway.

**The entry count is the second half of the defect and not a
restatement of the first.** `p_dying_entries` is incremented at the
top of `syscall_handler`, so it says the thread was in the kernel
with the mark set. The check that would have acted on it sits at the
end of the entry, and the entry blocks, so it is never reached. One
entry started, none finished, and the thread is still there.

**The wedged process is not left wedged, and the recovery is the
measurement.** A second kill ends it in 1.8 to 2.6 milliseconds
including the join. Nothing about the process changed between the two
kills except that its thread is now blocked, and a blocked thread is
what `thread_cancel` was built for. That difference is the whole of
the defect, and M20 stage five's workaround is the same observation
written as a way around it.

**The assertion is the wrong answer on purpose.** Stage one asserts
that the kill did *not* work, at the check and again in the report,
which is stage one of M20's shape: if the number is zero the
milestone has no subject and should be abandoned rather than built.
Stage two is what turns both over.

**The moment is constructed rather than hoped for.** Spawning and
killing inside one `sched_defer` is what makes the thread certainly
ready and certainly not yet run. Without it the server can reach its
receive first, and the check would be of a blocked thread, which is
the case that already works. The state is asserted at the kill rather
than assumed.

**Falsified two ways.** Reading the mark in `proc_user_start` before
dropping into user mode, which is stage two, fired `unrun: the kill
worked, so there is nothing to fix`. That also settles the question
stage two's *Watch for* raises, since ending a thread from the
trampoline neither faulted nor hung. Counting the entry on the way
out of `syscall_handler` rather than on the way in fired `kills: no
entry was started by a marked thread`, which is the difference
between the two placements made visible.

**And one falsification fired somewhere else.** Not counting entries
at all panicked in M17's own check first, `join spin: it did not
finish, or its exit advanced nothing`, because that check asserts the
same counter at zero. The floor this stage puts under the counter is
therefore not independently falsifiable, which is written here rather
than left to look stronger than it is.

**What the review found: the check could have measured the case that
works.** The state of the target was read before the kill and never
after it. Between the two the thread can be dispatched on the other
core, and a kill that lands on a thread which has reached its receive
is a kill that succeeds, so the check would have passed while testing
nothing. That is this milestone's *Watch for* clause exactly, and it
was written in the plan and then not obeyed a page later.

The state is now read again after the kill and before the core is let
go, which is the only moment where the answer means anything.
Falsified by letting the server run between the guard and the kill:
`unrun: the kill landed on state 2 with 1 points`.

**Ready is not the claim.** The check asserted the thread was
`THREAD_READY`, and a thread that ran and was preempted is ready too.
That one returns to user mode through a trap path which reads the
mark, so it is not the case this stage is about. The falsification
above proves the difference is real rather than theoretical: after two
yields the thread was still reported as ready, and the assertion that
caught it was the new one, that it has passed no preemption point. A
point is passed on the way into every entry, so a thread with none has
not been in the kernel on its own account.

**A thread was read through a pointer while it could be exiting.** The
poll walked to the process's first thread and read its state, from the
boot thread, holding none of the kernel's exclusion. A thread that
exits is taken off its process's list and its slot goes back to the
pool, and the whole point of this loop is that it runs while a thread
may be doing exactly that. It is the mistake M20 made three times and
its review found three times. One reading now happens under the kernel
lock with interrupts off, and what comes out is a copy: no pointer
survives the lock being put down.

**And a kill of a thread that never ran pokes nothing**, which is now
asserted here as well as reported. Poking a ready thread would not fix
anything, since a ready thread is on no core to be poked, and a change
that started doing it would have to say so in the compared report.
Making `proc_kill` poke every thread fires M17's own check first, `a
kill: it poked 1 cores for a thread that was not running`, so this
assertion is a restatement for a construction M17 does not cover
rather than an independent one, and it is written here as that.

**2. The mark on the way into user mode for the first time.**
*Planned.*

- *Check.* `proc_user_start` and `proc_thread_start` read the mark
  before dropping into user mode. A process killed between its spawn
  and its first instruction ends with the kill code, and the join
  returns inside a bound this check states rather than inside ten
  minutes. Stage one's assertion turns over.
- Both trampolines, and the check says which one it exercised: a
  program's first thread and a thread the program made are different
  paths and only the first is what M20 measured.
- Falsifiable by removing either check: the join runs out its
  deadline, which is the failure this stage exists to stop.

**What it settled.** Both trampolines read the mark. The compared
report, at both tiers:

```
  killed before ever running: 1, 1 a program and 0 a thread it made, 0 entries
  of those, found inside the kernel: 0
```

Stage one's two assertions are turned over rather than deleted. It
asserted that a kill at that moment reached nothing and that the
thread went on to start an entry anyway; what is asserted now is that
the kill reaches it, that it ends at a trampoline rather than
somewhere else, and that it starts no entry at all. A supervisor is
told the process has stopped 365 to 509 microseconds after asking,
against never.

**The third way into user mode.** The interrupt path, the fault path
and the system call path all call `proc_exit_if_dying`, and section
10.5's subsection lists the first two as where the mark is read. The
third is not a way back out of anything: `proc_user_start` and
`proc_thread_start` run in kernel mode on the new thread's own stack
and drop into user mode, and a thread that has never run has no trap
to return from. That is the whole defect, and the fix is one call in
each.

**The lock was the question the plan said to answer first, and the
answer is that it is not held.** `proc_exit_if_dying` is documented
as being called with the kernel lock held, because `thread_exit`
switches away and hands the lock to whichever thread runs next.
Measured over a boot, all 2557 arrivals at these trampolines found it
free: a dispatch is made with interrupts off and not with the lock.
So the check takes it when this core does not already hold it, which
is M20 stage three's arrangement for the same reason, and the other
branch is counted. It is zero in this boot, because nothing here
first-dispatches a thread from inside the kernel, and the count is in
the report so that the day something does, the line says so.

What is not restored is the interrupt state `klock_enter` returns.
Nothing comes back from there: the thread ends, and the thread that
runs next puts the lock down and the state back on its own way out,
which is the contract the trap paths already rely on.

**Both trampolines, counted apart.** Only a program's own first
thread is reached by anything in this boot, so the two counts are
separate and a check that added them together would not notice one
going missing. The second is stage five's construction, and until
then the line reads a zero that is honest rather than absent.

**Falsified, and one guard could not be.** Taking the check out of
the program's trampoline fired `join echoes: it did not finish, or
its exit advanced nothing`, which is the deadline running out and is
the failure the stage exists to stop. Taking out the lock
acquisition changed nothing this host can see: the boot completed
with the exit made from an unlocked trampoline. That guard is there
because the contract says so and because a first dispatch from inside
the kernel would need it, not because anything here demonstrates it,
and it is written down as that rather than counted as a check.

**What the review found: the mark was read outside the lock.** The
check read `p_dying` first and took the kernel lock afterwards, only
to end the thread. Every other reader of the mark reads it with the
lock held, and the order matters here more than anywhere: `proc_kill`
writes the mark and then reads the thread's state, declining to poke
one it finds ready, while this reads the mark after the thread has
been made running. Two cores each storing and then loading is the one
shape that can leave both reading the old value. The kill sends no
poke because it sees a ready thread, the trampoline sees no mark and
goes to user mode, and the thread runs on with nothing left to stop
it, which is the defect this milestone exists to remove arriving
again by a different route.

The lock is taken first and the mark read under it, which is an
acquire against the release that put the lock down. Reasoned rather
than observed: a store buffer losing a kill is not something a check
can provoke on demand, and the fix is the ordering rather than a
number.

**What that pairing does not cover.** It orders this against a kill
written inside the kernel, which is every kill a program makes.
`proc_kill` can also be called straight from a kernel thread, which
holds interrupts off and nothing else, and one check in M17 does
exactly that. Against that caller the mark is ordered by nothing.
Making `proc_kill` take the lock is not a safe change to make in
passing, because it calls `sched_undefer`, which can switch, and what
a thread holds when it is resumed is a convention this review is not
going to extend on the way past. It is the same residue M20 stage
three recorded and it is written down rather than closed.

**What the lock costs on the first dispatch of every thread.** Every
program start now takes it, 2557 times in a boot. Five burst runs
either side put the boot at 12.17 to 12.32 seconds with it and 11.99
to 12.37 without, so it is not separable from a spread of about four
tenths of a second on this host. At Tier 0 the lock is nothing at
all and the check compiles to the mark test.

**And the call sites said `false` and `true`.** Which trampoline a
thread is on is now said by passing the counter it belongs to, so the
call reads as what it does.

**3. The mark before an entry, and not only after it.** *Built.*

- *Check.* A marked thread does not begin an operation. Entries
  started while dying goes to zero and stays there, which is a count
  and belongs in the compared report; today it cannot be zero, because
  the check runs after the entry has already been executed.
- What this buys beyond stage two is the thread that is marked while
  it is in user mode and whose next call blocks. Stage two cannot
  reach it: it has already run.
- Falsifiable by moving the check back after the entry, which is the
  code as it stands.

**What it settled.** The mark is read before an entry runs and once
after a batch, in place of once after every entry. The compared line
at both tiers:

```
  stopped at an entry boundary: 70
```

Sixty-nine of those are the kills the rest of the boot writes, each
one reaching a thread that was inside an entry. The seventieth is
this stage's, and where each of them was stopped is printed above the
line:

```
  where a kill stopped a thread: 0 before a first entry, 1 before a
  later one, 69 after a batch
```

**The construction.** `twostep` sends two requests in one submission
to a channel nothing answers, so it blocks inside the first. The kill
cancels that wait, the first entry comes back interrupted, and the
second entry is the one that must never begin. Waited for rather than
timed: the check kills when the channel has a sender queued on it,
which is what says the program is inside the entry before the
boundary.

**Falsified by taking the boundary reading out.** With only the
reading after the batch, the second entry begins, sends to a channel
nobody receives on, and waits for ever: `join twostep: it did not
finish, or its exit advanced nothing`. That is the shape of stage
one's defect reached from inside a submission rather than from a
first dispatch.

**What the change buys and what this check does not reach.** Moving
the reading from after an entry to before the next one is the same
point for every entry but the first, so the boundary this check
exercises is one the old placement covered from the other side. What
is new is the reading before the *first* entry of a submission, and
it needs a thread that arrived at the kernel already marked.

Nothing in this boot produces one, and it is worth saying why rather
than leaving a zero. It takes a mark written while the thread is in
user mode, which takes another core, and then a trap of the thread's
own within the few microseconds before the kill's interrupt lands. A
program was written to make that likely, computing a stretch and then
making one request, killed from the other core over and over. It was
hit once in eight attempts, once in sixteen, and once in sixty-four,
which is a rate that reports the host rather than the kernel. The
program is kept in the shape that suits the deterministic
construction and the racing one is not in the boot.

**And the reading is what makes a kill orderable.** With the question
asked before the entry, a kill written under the kernel lock and an
entry taken under the same lock have two outcomes and no third: the
entry ran first and the thread is blocked where the cancel finds it,
or the mark is there to be read. Asked afterwards there is a third,
where the thread passes the mark's place, blocks, and the cancel has
already been and gone. That is the argument the change rests on, and
the boundary count is the part of it a check can hold.

**What the review found: the reading covered one of three ways out.**
The reading after the batch was at the end of the entry loop, and a
system call has three exits. A count that is not a count and an array
the caller cannot reach both return before any entry runs, and a
thread that arrived marked and asked for either would have gone back
to user mode with the mark unread. It is one reading in
`syscall_handler` now, after the body and before the return, which
covers all three. Not observable here, for the same reason the
first-entry boundary is not: reaching it needs a thread that arrived
already marked. Moving it back into the loop changes nothing this
boot can see, and that is written down rather than counted as a
check.

**A pointer to a channel the check no longer held.** The queue was
read through the `struct channel *` the check made, and the only
handle on it had been handed to the program. Since M20 that means a
program which exits early, which this one does if its namespace
lookup fails, takes the slot back with it, and the read would be out
of a slot something else has taken. The check keeps a handle of its
own now and closes it at the end.

**And that read was not synchronised.** The sender queue is a list
the other core puts threads on, and the answer decides when the kill
is written. It is read under the kernel lock with interrupts off, the
same way stage one's reading of a thread's state was fixed.

**4. A kill that finds every state at once.** *Built.*

- *Check.* One process, four threads, one in each of the states a kill
  has to reach: running on another core, ready and never run, blocked
  in a receive, and inside a kernel operation. All four end, the
  process is reaped, and the exit status is the kill code for each.
  The count of pokes says which of them needed one.
- Falsifiable per thread by removing the path that reaches that one:
  each failure names the state it left behind.

**What it settled.** Four mechanisms end a thread and until now each
was checked on a process that had one thread in one state. They work
together. `fourways` holds all four at once and the kill ends all
four:

```
a kill: four threads, one in each state it must reach
    the four it was about to reach         1 computing, 1 never run, 1 receiving, 1 inside
    threads the kill ended                 4 of 4, all with the kill's code
    pokes it had to send                   1
    from the kill to the join              about 4263 us
```

At Tier 0 the same lines read zero pokes. Nothing of the target is
running when the killer is running, so the state the poke is for does
not exist there and the mechanism is not tested. The time is the
host's and is printed above the compared line.

**The states, and what reaches each.** Blocked receiving, taken off
the channel's list by `thread_cancel`. Inside a request, the same
call, and the server it was talking to is told. Running on the other
core, the poke, and the mark read on the way back from the interrupt
it causes. Ready and never run, the mark read in the trampoline,
which is stage two. The fourth is why this stage is in M21 and not in
M17: before stage two a process arranged this way could not be killed
at all, because the thread that had not run would go on to user mode
and stay there.

**The arrangement is waited for, not assumed.** The four states are
counted in one walk under the kernel lock, and the check waits until
the count is the arrangement it wants before writing the kill. A
check that looked once would be checking the scheduler's timing. The
census distinguishes a thread that has never reached user mode from
one that has run and entered no system call, which needs a bit of
its own: `t_user_entered`, set by both trampolines. Without it the
thread that computes looks the same as the thread that has not
started, because neither has a preemption point to show.

**The reap needed a nudge, and that is not the kill's doing.** The
first version waited thirty seconds for the process to be reaped and
gave up. The threads had ended; one of them was parked on the second
core waiting to be collected, it holds a reference to its process,
and a core with nothing to run takes no dispatch, which is where
collection happens. The check gives that core one kernel thread to
dispatch. It is a property of how collection is scheduled rather than
of the kill, and it is written down here because this is the first
check in the system to end a process on a core that then has nothing
left to do.

**And the boot thread had to come off a channel.** The request that
leaves one thread inside a rendezvous is taken by the boot thread and
never answered. Left there, the boot thread would be serving that
channel for the rest of the run, which is section 19.3's unenforced
rule in its cross-channel form. The check answers after the join and
asserts the answer is refused, `SYS_ERR_STALE`, because the client is
gone. Refusing it is what takes the thread off the list.

**Falsified per state, by the counts rather than by a hang.** Two of
the four hang when their mechanism is removed. Skipping
`thread_cancel` for a thread waiting in a receive, and again for one
waiting for a reply, each leaves that one thread behind and the check
names it: `states: the kill left 0 computing, 0 never run, 1
receiving, 0 inside`, and the same with the last two counts swapped.
That reporting is the reason the stage waits for the threads itself
instead of leaving it to the join, which can say only that the
process did not finish.

The other two do not hang, and the compared report is what catches
them. Take out the poke and the thread that computes is still reached
by some later interrupt within the join's deadline, but a kill that
sent no poke is one fewer poke and one more thread stopped at an
entry boundary. Take out the trampoline reading and the thread that
has not run reaches user mode, makes its first call, and is caught at
the entry boundary instead: `killed before ever running` loses its
thread and `stopped at an entry boundary` gains one. So this stage
cannot falsify those two paths on its own, and says so. What it shows
is that each is the first thing to reach its state, and the compared
numbers say which reached which.

The thread that never runs receives on a channel nothing sends to
rather than computing, which is what makes the second of those
readable. A computing body ends too, reached by whatever interrupt
happens along, and the report then shows only that the thread was no
longer killed before running, without saying where it was caught.
Both were measured.

**What it cost.** Two channels, four threads and one more process in
the boot, and one more kill. The compared line at Tier 2:

```
  kills: 71 written, pokes 2, clients told 3
  killed before ever running: 1, 1 a program and 1 a thread it made, 0 entries
  stopped at an entry boundary: 72
```

The second line is the change worth naming. Stage two added a reading
in each of the two trampolines and only the program's had ever fired;
stage two guessed the other would come from stage five. It comes from
here. The thread `fourways` makes last is killed before the scheduler
reaches it, and it is the first thread in the system's history to be
stopped by the reading in `proc_thread_start`.

**What the review found: the line that said four was a constant.**
`threads the kill ended  4 of 4, all with the kill's code` was
printed from the constant, twice. Nothing read a thread's exit code,
and nothing counted the threads that ended: the process's status was
checked, and the process carries one code for all of them. The walk
that would have counted them finds an empty list, because a thread is
collected as soon as it ends and nothing holds it.

The check takes a reference on each of the four while all four are
still there, waits for each to reach dead, and compares its exit code
with the kill's. The line reports what that loop counted. It is also
what makes the per-state failure message reliable: the wait is per
thread rather than on a walk that can come up empty.

**And holding them found a race that frees a thread under a core.**
With the four held, the run faulted: `unhandled trap in nudge: page,
cause=0xc pc=0x0`. A thread writes `THREAD_DEAD` and then blocks for
the last time, and between the two it is dead and still running on
its own kernel stack. Dropping the last reference from another core
in that window collected it there and then, handed the slot back, and
the next thread built out of that slot was built over a stack a core
was still on.

The test for whether a dead thread may be collected was that it is
not the running thread and not the one this core has parked. Both of
those are about this core. `current` and the park slot are per core,
so a thread on the far side of its own dead write, or one parked on
the other core, passed both. The switch now says when it has finished
with a thread's stack, every dead thread is parked whether or not
something holds it, and nothing is collected before that word. The
last reference to go collects it, or the switch does, whichever is
later. Section 10.4 says so now.

Reachable without this check: any core closing the last handle to a
thread of another core while that thread is exiting. Nothing in the
boot did it, because nothing held a handle to a thread that was being
killed elsewhere. Falsifiable by putting the old test back, which
faults in the same place.

**One burst run in fifty did not come back.** It happened once, on
the run right after the collection fix went in, and it was the
machine failing to finish inside the session script's three minutes
rather than a panic or a mismatch. A burst run takes about thirteen
seconds. It has not happened again in forty-nine runs since, thirty
of them the burst alone, so what it was is not known and is written
here rather than left out.

**5. A thread made by a process that is already dying.** *Built.*

- *Check.* What `sys_thread_create()` does for a process that has been
  marked, which today is nothing special: the thread is created,
  becomes ready, and is a fresh instance of stage one's case. Either
  it is refused, or it is born and dies at stage two's check. The
  stage settles which and writes it in section 10.2.
- Falsifiable by the thread outliving the process, which is what makes
  a reap wait for ever.

**What it settled: it is refused.** A thread asked for in a process
that has been killed is refused with `SYS_ERR_OWNER_DEAD` and nothing
is built. The compared line at both tiers, in the form the review of
this stage left it:

```
  threads refused to a process that is over: 2, 1 of them never marked
```

Born and dying at stage two's reading was the other candidate and it
works, in the sense that the thread does end. What decides against it
is that it leaves the set of threads a kill has to reach open after
the kill is written. The kill's walk has been and gone, so the new
thread is not one the kill reached; it is one that reaches the same
end by another route, and a supervisor waiting for the process to be
over is waiting on something the process can still add to.

**And the measured case is worse than an argument about sets.** With
the refusal taken out, the create succeeds on a process whose last
thread had already gone, the thread runs, reads the mark in its
trampoline and exits, and the exit advances a completion that has
already been advanced: `panic: proc lastborn: completion advanced
twice`. The process had reported its exit and reported it again. That
is the falsification the stage's own plan asked for, in a sharper
form than the plan expected.

**The same call, twice, with the same arguments.** A refusal means
nothing unless the call works a moment earlier, which is stage one's
review applied here. The supervisor cannot invent the call: a thread
needs an entry point and a stack inside the target's own image, and
only the target knows where those are. So `lastborn` sends them. The
check builds a thread out of what it was sent, that thread runs and
says so on the same channel, and the only difference between that
answer and the refusal that follows the kill is the mark.

```
a kill: the thread a process that is over asks for
    a thread built from what it sent       ran and asked on the same channel
    and the same call after the kill       refused, with nothing made
    lastborn exited with status 3
    and one that nothing killed            refused the same, having ended itself
```

**What the construction found: the process argument was not used.**
`proc_thread_create(p, ...)` took a process and put the thread in the
caller's. `thread_alloc` attaches a new thread to the process of
whoever called, which is right for a kernel thread and right for this
call made from a thread of `p`, the only way it had ever been made.
Made from outside, it put the thread in the supervisor's own process
and the handle to it in `p`'s table. Section 10.2 has always said a
process with the right authority may create threads in another one,
so the signature was not wrong, the body was. It now puts the thread
where it was told. Falsifiable by putting it back, which leaves the
thread that was made unable to be found: `newborn: the thread that
was made: nothing was queued on lastborn recv`.

**A receive that blocks has no deadline.** Three checks in M21 waited
for a program's request in a loop with a deadline in it, around a
receive that blocks when there is nothing there. The deadline could
never fire: the loop does not come back to look at the clock. What
the machine did instead was stop, and the session script's three
minutes was the only thing that noticed. The wait is now for a sender
on the queue, which is a thing that can be given up on, and the
receive that follows has nothing to wait for.

**What it cost.** One more program in the boot, started twice, three
more threads between them, one more kill and one more channel.
Nothing in user mode reaches the refusal, and that is the reading
before an entry from stage three doing its job rather than an absence
of the case: a marked thread does not begin the operation. The count
stands on the check, which asks from outside the process.

**What the review found: a kill is only one of the two ways a
process ends.** The refusal read the mark, and a process that ends
on its own is never marked. So a supervisor could make a thread in a
process that had already exited and been joined, and the stage's own
argument about the set a kill has to reach says nothing about that
case at all.

Both halves of it were measured. The create succeeds, the thread is
added to a process whose exit has already been reported, and what
happens next depends only on whether anything had killed it. Marked,
the thread reads the mark in its trampoline, exits, and advances a
completion that has been advanced: `completion advanced twice`.
Unmarked, the thread simply runs, and the process it belongs to is
never reaped. Two seconds after the create, with the check watching:
one thread, in a process that had exited, and the channels still out.
That second one is exactly the falsification the stage's plan named,
"the thread outliving the process, which is what makes a reap wait
for ever", and the stage as built had not reached it.

The reading is now `p_dying || p_exited`, and the check asks a second
`lastborn` the same question. That one is answered rather than
killed, so it returns from its send, falls off the end of main, and
ends with nothing having been written against it. The same call is
refused the same way. Falsifiable by taking the second term out:
`newborn: a process that ended answered 0, not -10`.

The two are counted apart, because the reading was written for the
mark and did not see the exit:

```
  threads refused to a process that is over: 2, 1 of them never marked
```

**And the receive took a pulse for a request.** A server that
outlives a client is told so on the channel it was serving, and the
telling arrives through the same call as a request. This check kills
two clients and then waits for a third program to ask, so what came
back was `SYS_PULSE_DEAD_OWNER`, and the check read the makings of a
thread out of sixteen bytes that were eight: `newborn: the makings
were 8 bytes`. The receive drops pulses now and takes the request
behind them. It is also why the pulse line in the compared report
went back down by two: those two were being thrown away with the
channel at the end of the boot, and now they are delivered.

**6. M20's workaround comes out.** *Built.*

- *Check.* M20 stage five's restart loop sends a request and requires
  a reply before killing, and says in its own comment that this is
  what makes the kill defect moot. The request goes. Fifty-two servers
  are spawned and killed with no round trip in between, the channels
  come back, and the pool is where it started.
- This is the end-to-end statement of the milestone and the only stage
  that proves the fix is worth having rather than merely correct.
- Falsifiable by the loop hanging, which is what it did before the
  workaround was written.

**What it settled.** The round trip is gone and the loop runs. Fifty
two servers are started and killed, each one before it has ever been
on a core, and each channel comes back:

```
restarts: a server ended, and its channel with it
    servers started and ended unserved     52, all on slot 11
    and the pool where it started          12 in use, 14 at once
```

The kill is written inside the same deferred region as the spawn, so
the thread cannot have run in between. That is not a convenience. It
makes the case deterministic instead of leaving it to the scheduler,
and a count that moves on its own is a count that cannot go in a
compared file. The compared line at both tiers:

```
  killed before ever running: 53 a program and 1 a thread it made, 0 entries
```

Fifty two of those fifty three are this loop. The other is stage
one's check, and the thread is stage four's idler.

**And two other numbers moved, both downwards.** Threads stopped at
an entry boundary went from seventy four to twenty two, because the
fifty two servers used to be killed while blocked in a receive and
now they never reach one. The first field of the same line used to
be a count kept by stage one's check of the kills it had written
against a thread that had never run. It is gone: the kernel counts
that properly now, in two places, and a check keeping its own tally
of a kernel property was a leftover from the stage where the kernel
kept none.

**What the loop no longer has.** The client connection went with the
round trip it was for. What is left is the arrangement section 18.3
describes with nothing else in it: a supervisor holds the only handle
there is, gives it to the server, kills the server, and the channel
goes with the process. The one holder is asserted inside the deferred
region, before the server can run, end and be collected, because
after that the pointer would name a slot something else had taken.

**Falsified twice, and the first attempt was wrong about which
reading matters.** Taking out stage two's reading in the trampoline
does not hang the loop. The server goes on into user mode, calls
`sys_msg_recv`, and stage three's reading before an entry stops it
there instead, which the report says exactly:

```
  where a kill stopped a thread: 52 before a first entry, 1 before a
  later one, 21 after a batch
```

That is the boundary stage three said it could not construct. Its
entry records a racing program hit once in eight attempts, once in
sixteen and once in sixty four, and says the case needs a thread that
arrives at the kernel already marked. This loop makes fifty two of
them, deterministically, and the only reason the number is zero in a
working kernel is that the trampoline gets there first.

So the two readings are a backstop for each other, and what the loop
needs is that at least one of them is present. With both gone it
hangs at round zero, which is what M20 saw: `join echoes: it did not
finish, or its exit advanced nothing`.

**What it cost.** Nothing added. The loop is shorter by a connection,
a send and a handle, and the boot is shorter by fifty two round
trips.

**What the review found: the count of servers was the loop counter.**
`ended` was incremented once a round, so the reported number said the
loop had gone round fifty two times and nothing else. It now asks,
once a round, that the count of programs killed before ever running
went up by exactly one, and counts the rounds where it did. A total
that came out right at the end of the boot with one round having
taken another way out would not have shown.

**And the checks were entries that did not take the kernel lock.**
Every entry in this system arrives from a vector, which takes the
kernel lock on the way in and drops it on the way out. The entries a
check makes arrive from a kernel thread, which holds nothing, and
they ran the same operations with the exclusion missing.

What that cost was a join that hung. A wait on a completion reads the
timeline, finds it short of the value, and puts itself on the waiter
list; the advance on the other core writes the value and walks that
list. Those two interleave in one order that loses the wake, and the
waiter is left on a list nobody will look at again. Measured at about
one burst run in twelve: a thirty second timeout on a process that
had already exited, all four threads gone, the timeline sitting at
the value being waited for. Three failures in forty runs before, none
in forty after. This is also what the single unexplained burst
failure in stage four's review was.

**And the aarch64 interrupt return did not put back what it saved.**
The vector a program's interrupt arrives on saves `elr_el1` and
`spsr_el1` into its frame and never restored them. It ereted on
whatever those registers held, which is right only while nothing has
taken an exception in between. That handler is exactly where
something does: waking a thread that outranks the interrupted one
switches away from inside it, and whatever runs next takes traps of
its own, each writing both registers. The program then came back from
its interrupt at another thread's address, in another thread's mode.

It was found from the far end. A thread whose whole body is
`for (;;) { n++; }` exited with the code its library uses when an
entry function returns, and a receive that nothing had sent to came
back. The riscv64 port states the rule in its own trap path, that the
return state goes in the frame and not left in the registers because
a handler may switch; this port had written the saving half and not
the restoring half. It leaves through the same tail as a system call
now, which is where that restore already lived.

**And a thread that was supposed never to run, ran.** `fourways`
made the thread for the fourth state itself, last, behind a thread
that never yields, and said that it therefore sits on the queue for
the life of the process. It does not. A thread preempted by
something that outranks it goes to the back of its own level, so the
first time the supervisor woke to look, the one that computes landed
behind the one that must not run, and the next time the supervisor
slept it ran. Measured at about one run in twenty five, on top of the
other two.

A program at the lowest priority cannot arrange for anything below
it, and everything this program has is at that priority. So the
arrangement moved to the side that can arrange it: the fourth thread
is made by the check, out of an entry point and a stack the program
sends the way `lastborn` does, inside the deferred region that also
carries the kill. That is this stage's own discipline applied to
stage four, and it makes the state exact rather than likely: the
thread is made, counted, and killed with nothing having had a chance
to dispatch it.

**What the three together were worth.** The check that found all of
this is one program, on one port, at one tier: about five failures in
a hundred and fifty runs of the paced session on aarch64 at Tier 0,
in three different shapes. With the three fixes in, seventy runs and
none. The rate is the host's and the shapes are the kernel's.

**And a sweep for more of the same three.** Each of the three had a
shape rather than a location, so the rest of the system was read for
the shape.

*A trap path that saves what it does not put back.* One instance, the
one that was found. The riscv64 port routes every `sret` through one
restore and says why in a comment; the aarch64 port's other three
handlers all restore, and one of them carries the same warning about
a handler that switches. Neither port saves floating-point state and
neither needs to: everything is built `-mgeneral-regs-only`. The
per-core register is written once at boot on both ports and is not
reachable from user mode.

*An entry made without the kernel lock.* The harness was one caller;
the calls under it were more. `channel_send`, `channel_recv`,
`channel_reply`, `timeline_wait`, `thread_cancel` and `proc_kill`
each read a state another core owns and then join or walk a list, and
each was reached from the boot's kernel threads with interrupts off
and nothing else. They take the lock themselves now when it is not
already held, which costs an entry from user mode nothing and makes
a kernel thread's call the same kind of thing as an entry.

Only the first of those was measured failing, as the join that timed
out. The others are the same read-then-join against the same
writer, and that is written here as an argument rather than as a
measurement. One of them closes something already written down: M21
stage two's review recorded that a kill written by a kernel thread
was ordered against the trampoline's reading by nothing, and left it
open because only the reading side had been fixed. `proc_kill` takes
the lock now, which is the writing side.

The pools are not in this list and do not need to be: they have a
lock of their own, which is why an allocation from a kernel thread
was never the problem.

*A number that is a constant wearing a measurement's clothes.* The
boot prints a hundred and seventy four of these lines. The ones that
print a constant print the experiment's own parameters, which is what
they are for: how many cycles were spent, how many slots the pool
has, how many departures were made. The counters behind the rest are
incremented where something was observed rather than once a round.
The one that was not is the one this review started with.

**7. What it cost, and section 10.5 written to it.** *Built.*

- *Check.* The figures as counts: kills that reached a thread that had
  never run, entries started while marked, and the pokes, against what
  M17's three counts already report.
- Section 10.5's subsection on who a kill reaches is rewritten. It
  currently says the mark is read "where a trap returns to user mode"
  and lists the two trap paths; there is a third way into user mode
  and it did not look. Section 10.2 gains what happens to a thread
  created by a dying process.

**What it settled: the doors are countable and they add up.** The
milestone's claim is that a kill reaches every thread of its target.
That is now an arithmetic statement the boot makes about itself. A
kill closes the set of threads it has to reach at the moment it
writes the mark, because nothing can be added to a process that is
over. Every thread in that set ends, and the compared lines say
where:

```
  threads a kill had to reach: 81, and all of them ended
  by one of three doors: 54 a trampoline, 22 an entry boundary, 4 a trap, 1 already leaving
```

At Tier 0 the same lines read 79 reached and 2 at a trap. The
difference is the two threads that were computing on the second core
when they were killed, which is the state that exists only there.

**The three doors are section 10.5's sentence turned into a sum.**
The trampoline is the way into user mode that had no reading before
stage two, and fifty four of the eighty one leave by it: fifty two
are stage six's restart loop, one is stage one's check, and one is
the thread stage four has never dispatched. The entry boundary is
where a thread inside a submission stops, twenty two of them. The
trap is the interrupt or fault a computing thread is reached by, and
the poke is what makes that trap happen on another core.

The last number is not a door and is reported rather than folded in.
It is a thread that was already inside its own exit when the mark
went down, which is what a thread that faults and halts its cohort
does to itself: the halt kills the process the thread belongs to, and
the kill counts a thread that is on its way out already. Folding it
into the sum would make the sum hold whatever happened.

**And what the accounting has that the three counts alone do not.**
Each count can be right on its own while a thread leaves some other
way, and a fourth way out is exactly what this milestone was about.
For M17 and M20 there was one door: a thread that arrived at none of
them was a thread a kill did not reach, and no number said so because
nothing counted the set it belonged to.

Two of the three readings have been taken out and measured. Without
the one in the trampoline the split moves rather than breaking, which
stage six's review records: the thread reaches user mode, makes its
first call, and the boundary catches it there instead, one fewer at
a trampoline and one more at a boundary. Without the one on the way
back from an interrupt, stage four's check reports the kill leaving
three threads computing and gives up. So the split is what the
compared file holds, and the sum is what says no thread left by
something that is not on the list.

**What M17's three counts say now.** Kills written went from
seventeen to seventy two, which is stage six's loop and nothing
about the kernel. Pokes stayed at two: a poke is per running thread
of a target, and the boot has two of those. Clients told their
server had gone stayed at three. What is new beside them is the
whole accounting above, and the two lines that say a marked thread
starts no operation and that nothing is made in a process that is
over.

**Section 10.5 is written to it.** Its subsection said the mark is
read "where a trap returns to user mode" and named the two trap
paths. There are three ways into user mode and the third is not a
return from anything: a thread that has just been made runs a
trampoline in kernel mode and drops into user mode without having
trapped. The section says so, says that the entry-boundary reading
is before an entry rather than after it and why the order matters,
and states the closed set and its three doors. The paragraph arguing
that one core needs no poke is corrected as well: its reasoning was
that a thread being killed is either where it was interrupted or
where it blocked, and a thread that has never run is in neither
place.

Section 10.2 gained what happens to a thread created in a process
that is over, which stage five settled and its review widened to
cover a process that ended without being killed.

*Done when* a kill reaches a thread that has never run, a marked
thread starts no operation, a kill of a process with threads in every
state ends all of them, and M20 stage five's restart loop kills its
servers without first asking them for anything.

**What the review found: the fourth number was the remainder of the
other three.** The line reads as four numbers that add up to a total,
and one of them was the total minus the other three. A remainder adds
back up whatever either side is, so the sum said nothing: it was the
same shape as the count of servers this milestone's sixth stage had
already been caught printing.

A thread now carries whether it is ending because it read the mark,
set by each of the three places that read it and by nothing else, and
`thread_exit` counts a thread that ends while its process is marked
without that flag. The five numbers come from five places and the
line between them is arithmetic. The numbers did not move, which is
what says the remainder had been right.

**And the set the kill counts no longer includes threads that had
already ended.** A thread stays on its process's list until it is
collected, so the walk that counts what a kill has to reach was
counting dead ones too. There is nothing there to cancel and no core
to poke, and a kill that counted one would have been short by it for
the rest of the boot. Nothing in this boot kills a process with a
dead thread still on its list, so the number is the same either way;
it is a correctness fix by reading rather than a measured one, and
it is written down as that.

**What the accounting catches, and what it does not.** The invariant
with teeth is that every thread a kill had to reach ended, and
anything that breaks it leaves a thread running, which a join
notices first. What the split adds is the shape of a way out that
nobody counted: a new path into user mode added without a reading
would show up as a thread that ended its own way, and that number is
in the compared file. It is a statement the boot makes about itself
rather than a trap that springs first, and it is worth having for
the same reason the channel accounting in M20 was.

**A comment that described code that is not there.** Stage one's
check said the process it wedges is recovered by a second kill,
which was true when the first kill reached nothing. Stage two turned
that over and the second kill went with it; the comment stayed.

*Would falsify.* That the trampoline is the right place to look.
 If
reading the mark there is unsafe, because the thread is in kernel mode
on its own stack outside the kernel's exclusion and `thread_exit` from
there is not the same as `thread_exit` from a trap, then the answer is
that the mark has to be read on the far side, at the first entry the
thread makes, and a thread killed before it ever calls anything cannot
be reached at all. That would be a smaller milestone and a worse
system, and section 10.5 would have to say so.

*Watch for.* A check that cannot fail, which is now eight consecutive
milestones. The shape here is specific: every stage's check depends on
winning a race with a thread that is about to run, and a check that
kills too late measures nothing while looking exactly like one that
passes. Every construction has to assert the state of the target at
the moment the kill goes in, the way M20 stage five learned to, rather
than assuming the scheduler did what the check wanted.

And a fix that moves the problem. Ending a thread before it reaches
user mode means ending it somewhere `thread_exit` has never been
called from. What holds at that point, what the trampoline has on its
stack, and whether the kernel lock is held are three separate
questions, and stage two answers them before it writes anything.

*Size.* Small. Two checks in two trampolines and one check moved from
after an entry to before it. The measurement around them is most of
the work, as it has been for five milestones, and stage four is the
one that is neither small nor known in advance.

---

### M22. The Reply a Thread Still Owes

**A server thread records one client and may owe several.**

**Done.** All seven stages are built. Section 25 says what it
answered, what it cost, what the building kept finding, and what it
left untested. What it replaced was a field that counts to one, read
by four milestones of accounting and checked against the only server
this boot had.

A receiving thread now holds the set of clients it owes, and the
serving entry on a channel is the request rather than the thread that
took it. A donation goes back to the highest priority still owed
rather than to base at the first reply. A thread inside requests on
two channels is on both lists. A client that dies while its request
is held leaves the set and the list, and a channel with a request
standing in it is not freed. An exit releases every client the thread
owes rather than the one its record named.

```
  a server thread owed more than one reply: 205, and at most 2 at once
  a record that holds one: 5 written over, and a set that kept 5 of them
  a donation given back: 4 stopped above base, 0 left to another core
  a request taken on a channel its thread was already serving another on: 1
  a request in flight when its client died: 17, and a slot kept for one: 2
  a death that reached every client it owed: 2 released at once at most, and 1 left to the owner's
  what the set costs a rendezvous: 0 steps in 200 owing one, 200 in 200 owing two
```

The last line is the falsification clause answered. A rendezvous
against a set of n walks n - 1 entries, because the request being
answered is at the head and what is walked is whatever was there
before it, so a server owing one walks nothing. Section 12.6 gains
what a receiving thread may owe and what bounds it, and section 12.3's
chain walk is stated against the requests a channel names.

`t_client` is one identifier, `t_donor` is one pointer, and
`t_serve_ch` and `t_serve_next` are one channel and one link. Between
them they are the whole of what the kernel knows about a receiving
thread being inside a request, and each of them counts to one. A second
rendezvous on the same thread overwrites all four.

**Section 12.6 describes the shape that needs more than one.** It says
a server may "receive on one thread and hand the client id to a
worker", and section 12.2 says any thread of a server may reply, which
is what makes that legal. A dispatcher with one receiving thread and
four workers has four outstanding requests and one `t_client`. The
section says which structure to choose and what each costs, and nothing
anywhere says the kernel can record only the first.

**The tree already does it.** The console's request thread receives a
read, finds no line to return, holds the request rather than answering
it, and goes back to receive. The next request overwrites the held
client's identifier. It survives because a reply is addressed by
identifier and this one comes from the other thread, which is section
12.2 working, and because M20 taught `serving_begin` to notice the
channel it is already on. Both of those handle the symptom.

**What the overwrite costs, in three places.**

*The record names the wrong client.* `t_client` is what a reply from
this thread checks itself against, what says whether a wake was a
request or a pulse, and what M18's departure handling and M21's kill
accounting read when they ask what a thread was doing.

*The donation goes back at the first reply rather than the last.*
`undonate` is documented as running "now that it owes nobody anything",
and it runs when the thread replies to whoever it most recently
received from. A thread holding a request from a high-priority client
and answering a low-priority one drops to its base priority with the
first client still waiting. Not visible in this boot, because every
program the shell spawns inherits the shell's priority and a donation
between equals raises nothing.

*The serving list has one entry for a thread that may be inside two
channels, and one link field for every list.* Holding on one channel
and receiving on another writes `t_serve_ch` and `t_serve_next` while
the thread is still linked into the first channel's list, so the first
list runs into the second. `README.md` has carried that as worse if it
happened since M20 found the same field pointing at itself.

**And M20's free test reads that list.** A channel's slot goes back
when nothing holds it and nobody is standing in it, and
`c_serving == NULL` is how the second half is asked. A server that
holds one request and replies to another leaves `c_serving` at that
reply, while its held client is still REPLY-blocked with that channel
in `t_blocked_on` and on none of the channel's lists. The server's
entry was the only thing representing that client, and it has gone.
That is a channel freed under a thread waiting on it, reachable by a
program that can be written today.

**What makes this worth a milestone rather than a fix.** Four
milestones have built accounting on a field that counts to one.
Section 12.3's chain walk, M18's departure notices, M20's channel
lifetime and its walk, and M21's kill accounting all read the
server-side record, and every one of them was checked against a server
with one outstanding request, because that is the only server the boot
has. The fix is a list. Finding out what each of those four says when
the number is two is not.

*Needs.* Nothing missing. Each outstanding client is already blocked,
already carries `t_donee` pointing at the thread serving it, and is
already its own record. What does not exist is the link the other way
for more than one of them.

**What this is not.** Not a worker pool and not asynchronous message
passing: a request is still served by a thread running at the client's
priority, and section 2.4 does not move. Not a change to who may reply,
which section 12.2 settles. Not a new bound, since the thread pool is
already one: a client appears on at most one of these lists and there
are `SYS_MAX_THREADS` of them.

**1. What a thread owes, counted.** *Built.*

- *Check.* The boot reports the greatest number of clients any
  receiving thread owed at once, and what the kernel's record named at
  that moment. Asserted to disagree, because if they agree the
  milestone has no subject. The count goes in the compared report at
  both tiers.
- The number comes from the recorded shell session rather than from a
  program written to produce it. The console holds a read and receives
  again in every session with a line typed at it, which is what M20
  found by walking a list that did not end.
- Also counted: replies sent to a client the replying thread's record
  did not name. That is section 12.2 working as specified and is the
  reason nothing has noticed, so it is measured before anything is
  changed.
- Falsifiable by the case not reproducing, which would mean the console
  does not do what M20 found it doing.

**What it settled.** The milestone has a subject. Two lines in the
compared report at each tier:

```
  a server thread owed more than one reply: 1 time, at most 2 at once
  a record that holds one: 1 written over, 2 off a serving list still owing
```

and a block above the line, where the first four move with when console
input arrives and the last is the walk the review added:

```
what a server thread owes, against what it records
    held a request and blocked receiving   19
    replies its record did not name        16
    left on a serving list by a reply      16
    on a serving list at the end           5, 2 of them owing nobody
    every count against a walk of clients  19 threads, all agreeing
```

**The case is not the console's, which is what the plan assumed.** The
console does hold a read with no line behind it and go back to receive,
nineteen times in a paced session, and that is what the plan expected to
produce a thread owing two. It does not. Nothing sends the console a
second request while it is holding one, because the only client talking
to it across a held read is the shell and the shell is the thread
blocked on that read. The one thread in the boot that owed two replies
at once is the boot thread inside M21 stage five's check, which receives
from a program and then from a thread that program made. The plan's
sentence about the console was about a different symptom of the same
field, and this is written here rather than quietly replaced.

**The record stops naming what is owed in two ways and both happen.**
One rendezvous wrote `t_client` over an identifier the thread still
owed. Nineteen receives cleared it on the way into the block, because
after the block it is what tells a request from a pulse. The field has
two jobs and the second takes it from the first, so the count of
overwrites is not the whole of how often the record goes.

**Sixteen replies were sent by a thread whose record did not name the
client.** That is section 12.2 working exactly as specified: the
identifier addresses the reply and any thread of the server may send
one. It is also the reason nothing has noticed the record being wrong,
and it is measured before anything is changed.

**The serving list is wrong in both directions, and the second was not
in the plan.** Two threads came off a channel's serving list while still
owing a client on it, which is the hazard the plan named:
`channel_free_if_idle` reads that list for whether anybody is standing
in a channel. Sixteen times a thread was left *on* a list owing nobody,
because `serving_end` runs on whichever thread replies and the console
answers a held read from the thread that has the bytes. The boot ends
with two threads standing in channels they are serving nothing on, and
the second of them is there for a third reason again: `wedge`'s client
was released without the server being taken off the list.

**What could not be asserted, and why.** Three of the four numbers above
the line are zero in the burst session. The line is always ready there,
the request thread answers where it stands, and no reply comes from
another thread of the server. Asserting them above zero passed the paced
run and stopped the burst one, which is a check measuring the harness
rather than the kernel. Only the count of threads that held a request
and went back to receive is above zero in both, and it is the only one
of the four that is asserted.

**The count is checked against a walk.** Where the count passes one,
every thread is walked and those pointing at this server are counted,
and a disagreement panics. That happens once in a boot, which is worth
less than M20's four walks; the review is what widened it to every
thread at the end of the boot as well.

**Falsified six ways.** Not decrementing the count when a client stops
being owed fired the walk, `a thread owes 2 and 1 threads say so`. Not
letting the greatest pass one, not counting the overwrite, not counting
a thread that leaves the serving list owing, not counting the walk, and
not counting a thread left on a list owing nobody each fired their own
assertion by name.

**And one assertion that could not fail was written and removed.** That
the threads owing nobody are no more than the threads standing, which is
arithmetic: the first is counted inside the branch that counts the
second.

**What it costs on the rendezvous.** One increment and one branch, with
the walk behind a test that is true once in a boot. The best round trip
was 445 to 591 ticks over three runs before and 451 to 696 after, which
is inside the spread of the host and says the store is not separable
from it.

**What the review found: the walk read every thread with nothing
held.** It runs on the boot thread after the session, and the session
does not take everything with it. The console and `wedged` are still
there, and at Tier 2 the other core can be inside a rendezvous writing
the two fields being read. Confirmed rather than argued: an assertion
that the kernel lock was held fired at Tier 2. That is M20 stage
three's review finding arriving again about a different walk, and the
fix is the same one, take the lock where this core does not already
hold it and turn interrupts off inside it.

**And the count was checked at one moment, for one thread.** The walk
inside the rendezvous runs where the count passes one, which happens
once in a boot. It says nothing about the other thirty-one slots and
nothing about the nineteen times a thread owed exactly one. Every
thread's count is now checked against the clients pointing at it at the
end of the boot as well, 19 threads in a paced run and 20 in a burst
one, all agreeing. Falsified by adding one to a single thread's tally,
which fired `owed: console owes 0 and 1 threads say so`.

**A guard that turned a wrong count into a plausible one.** The
decrement refused to go below zero, which is exactly the failure the
walk exists to catch, hidden at the site where it would first be
visible: a thread owing fewer than the clients pointing at it is a
channel that reads as free to go with somebody still standing in it. It
panics now, and the panic fires in none of the eight runs. Falsified by
dropping twice, which fired `channel: lastborn stops being owed by
boot, which owes nothing`.

**A number in the compared report that meant something looser than it
said.** The overwrite test was that the record is not empty and the
thread owes somebody, and those two being true does not make the
recorded identifier one of the clients owed: a record can name a client
that gave up at its deadline while the thread owes a different one. It
is a lookup and a test of the named client's own record now.

Reasoned rather than measured, and written down as that: the loose test
gives the same 1 in this boot, because nothing here has two outstanding
clients and one of them giving up. What it cost is nothing the host can
separate, with the best round trip at 442 to 471 ticks over three runs
against 445 to 591 before the stage.

**And the interpretation of the two that left a serving list was
checked rather than asserted.** Both of them left the list empty behind
them, `stale-wait` on the `stale` channel and `echoes` on its own,
which is what makes `channel_free_if_idle` able to answer its question
with the wrong answer. Measured at the site rather than inferred from
the count.

*Left for stage six.* A server that exits owing more than one releases
only the client its record names. The others keep `t_donee` pointing at
a thread that is about to be freed, and the count on that thread is
left standing. Nothing in this boot reaches it: a drop whose thread had
already died or gone was counted and is zero in all eight runs.

**2. The set of clients a thread owes.** *Built.*

- *Check.* A server thread that owes two clients names both, and the
  count from stage one agrees with a walk. The set is a list threaded
  through the clients, headed on the server thread: section 12's own
  principle is that the blocked sender is the queue slot, and a client
  waiting for a reply is exactly that.
- `t_client` becomes the head of it. What it meant before survives as
  the question of whether the list is empty, and the two places that
  used it to tell a request from a pulse have to say which they meant.
- Falsifiable by dropping the link on the second rendezvous, which is
  the code as it stands: the walk and the count disagree and stage one's
  assertion comes back.
- *Watch for.* The rendezvous path is the hottest in the kernel and
  this adds a store to it. The cost is measured against M20's figure
  for the same path.

**What it settled.** A thread names every client it owes. A third line
in the compared report at each tier:

```
  and a set that holds them all: 1 of 1 the record lost
```

and two more above it, where the walk is new and the count of blocks is
the host's:

```
    count, list and walk at the end        19 threads, all agreeing, about 205 us
    the set kept what a block gave away    19 of 19
```

**`t_client` did not become the head of the list, which is what the
plan said it would.** The field has a second job the plan did not
account for: after a receive that blocked, it is what says which kind
of wake this was, a sender having filled it in and a pulse having left
