for and not what anything here demonstrates.

**Every leaf being non-global.** Both ports' by-name invalidation is
safe only because no mapping is marked global. Two addresses are
checked, one in a program and one in the kernel's identity mapping, and
the claim is about all of them.

**More than two cores.** Every count here comes from `-smp 2`.

---

## 23. Milestone 20, in Retrospect

M20 set out to make a channel's slot come back. Every other pool in
this system returned what it lent and this one never had: a boot ended
with 40 channels in use of 48 and a high-water mark of 40, which is
what a pool nothing gives back to looks like. M17 had already paid for
it once, running out of channels in an unrelated check, and had
written the sentence this milestone acted on. The mechanism was
smaller than expected and the checks around it were not, which is now
the fifth milestone to cost more to measure than to build.

### 23.1 The Questions

**Can all the holders be found?**

Yes, and the walk says so four times a boot. The count the kernel
keeps is compared against a walk of every process handle table, every
connection, every thread and every slot: 10 tables, 32 connections, 32
threads and 48 slots, about 57 microseconds warm and 767 the first
time, with the kernel held. The four walks have never disagreed, and
the falsification clause said that if they could not be made to agree
nothing after stage two was safe to build.

Two holders are counted and three more stand in a channel without
being counted. A handle and a connection hold it; a thread queued to
send, a thread blocked receiving and a thread inside a request stand
in it and are read from the channel's own lists. What does not hold a
channel is a pointer the kernel keeps, which stage three found out by
freeing channels the boot still had pointers to.

**Does the slot come back?**

612 channels are made in a boot and 589 go back, against 40 made and
none going back before this. **The high-water mark fell from 40 to
24**, which is what the pool would have to be sized for, and used ends
below it for the first time in this system's life.

**Is `SYS_MAX_CHANNELS` a bound on how many exist at once?**

Yes. The boot makes 612 channels on a pool of 48, 512 of them in one
check that holds eight at a time and runs sixty-four times, and the
pool comes back to where it started after every cycle. A server is
restarted 52 times, four more than the pool has slots, every one of
them on the same slot.

**What does the counting cost on the path that cannot afford one?**

Nothing measurable. The count is a branch in the handle retain and
release path, which four other types already take, and one question at
the end of a receive, a reply and a send. The send is the hot one: the
best round trip in the boot was 888 ticks before that wrapper and 875
after, which is inside the run-to-run spread. What it cost in space is
13 to 20 kilobytes of text, almost all of it the checks, and 512 bytes
of bss.

**Was section 8 wrong?**

Not wrong, incomplete, and the gap was the whole milestone. It bought
one property, that kernel memory is a function of the configuration
and not of the workload, and that property is worth nothing on its
own: a pool that never takes an object back has a fixed footprint and
still stops at a date set by its history. Section 8 now states the
half it was missing, that a pool's size bounds how many objects exist
at one time and not how many may ever be made, and names the channel
as the exception that was. Section 12 gained 12.8, which says what a
channel's lifetime is and what ends it, and which the specification
had never said anywhere.

### 23.2 What It Cost

**Fifteen commits, eleven files, 3521 lines added and 35 removed**,
of which 2293 are code, 1218 are documentation and ten are the
compared reports.

**Three fifths of the code is the measurement.** `init_main.c`
accounts for 1379 of those lines against 762 in `kern_channel.c` and
152 across two headers, `kern_objref.c` and `kern_lock.c`. The
mechanism is a count on the channel, two functions to move it, one to
ask whether the slot can go, and three wrappers. The rest is the walk
that checks the count and the seven stages of checks that exercise it.

**13 to 20 kilobytes of text**, 415954 to 429220 on riscv64 at Tier 0
and 549860 to 570068 on aarch64 at Tier 2, the larger figures being
the tier that runs more of the checks.

**About 512 bytes of bss** at every configuration: a hold count on
each of 48 channels, six counters, and one reading of the pool kept
for the report.

**Two lines in the compared report** in place of one, and they are the
same paced and burst at each tier.

**About half a second of boot**, 11.4 to 11.6 seconds to 12.0 to 12.1
on riscv64 measured on the burst session, most of it the 52 spawns and
kills of the restart loop and 63 milliseconds of the 512-channel loop.
The aarch64 burst session finishes inside the harness's fixed
five-second tail at both revisions and says nothing about this.

### 23.3 What the Building Kept Finding

**Checks that read through a pointer the check is about.** Three
separate times: both wrappers held a channel pointer across an
operation that blocks, the restart loop read a hold count through the
pointer it had kept, and the same pattern would have reported a pass
in exactly the case each was built to detect. The rule this milestone
leaves behind is that a path which frees objects must hold identifiers
and not pointers across anything that can block, and that a check for
a premature free is the last place to read through a raw pointer.

**Assertions that could not fail.** Stage six asserted that the
channels it had spent equalled the cycles times the number per cycle,
which is arithmetic. Stage three's check that a recycled slot comes
back empty could not be falsified at all, because taking the clear out
of `pool_alloc` stops the boot thousands of lines earlier. Both are
written down as what they are rather than counted as checks.

**Checks that could not fail because an earlier one fires first.**
Stage six's two obvious falsifications, removing the free and leaking
one in sixteen, were both caught by stage four's four-channel check
long before a five-hundred-channel loop saw them. To falsify stage six
at all the defect had to be scoped to the channels it spends. That is
the checks working, and it is worth knowing that a later stage's
falsification may say more about an earlier stage than about itself.

**A list that loops, found by bounding a walk.** The console channel's
serving list pointed at itself, because a thread that takes a second
request on a channel it is already serving is put on the list twice.
The first version of the walk did not come back and printed nothing; a
walk bounded by the number of threads in the machine panicked with
which list it was on. A diagnostic that hangs is worse than one that
says what it found.

**A defect found by writing the specification.** Section 12.8 had to
list the ways a thread leaves a channel. There are three, the code's
own comment said three, and only two of them asked whether the slot
could go. A channel whose holders all went while a thread was queued
on it was given back when that thread was served and leaked when it
gave up. Nothing in five stages of checks had looked, because stage
four released its sender by receiving, which is the path that works.

**Exclusion that interrupts-off does not buy.** Stage three's free
tested three lists and a pulse count with interrupts off and nothing
else, on a kernel thread that holds none of the kernel's exclusion, so
the other core could have been putting a thread on one of the lists
being tested. The test and the free now happen under the kernel lock,
and so does the walk.

### 23.4 What Is Still Untested

**A channel freed on one core while another is inside it.** Every
wrapper holds an identifier across the block precisely for this, and
nothing in this boot exercises the window. The same is true of stage
three's lock guard: it exists for a path that will exist.

**Giving a slot back from inside a system call.** One of 589 frees in
a boot happens on a core already holding the kernel lock, and that one
arrived only with the send wrapper added in the last review. Before
it, the count was zero, and the branch that does not take the lock was
never taken.

**The cross-channel form of the double-serving limitation.** A thread
serving one channel that takes a request on another does not happen in
this boot, and the count of serving entries left behind is zero in all
eight combinations of port, tier and mode. If it did happen it would
be worse than a stale name: `t_serve_next` is one field shared by
every serving list, so the first list would run into the second.

**A kill that is accepted and does nothing.** Killing a process whose
thread is ready and has never run leaves it alive: the mark is set,
nothing is blocked to cancel, and the thread then runs and blocks in a
receive that never asks whether its process is dying. Measured, not
fixed, and not this milestone's to fix.

**A channel held by a connection kept for reaping.** A server that
dies with uncollected connections leaves a channel those connections
hold and nothing will ever collect. The end-of-boot assertions do not
see it, because holds is above zero and the slot counts as reachable.
It shows only as a slot still in use.

**Pool exhaustion under work.** The boot proves it can spend 612
channels on 48 slots. What a system does when it is short of channels
while doing something other than proving it can run out is not
answered, and the check that would answer it is the one M17 hit by
accident.

**More than two cores, and real hardware.** Every count here comes
from `-smp 2` under an emulator.

---

## 24. Milestone 21, in Retrospect

M21 set out to fix a kill that a thread could outlast. A process killed
before its first thread had run was not killed: the mark went down,
nothing was blocked to cancel, and the thread then ran, entered user
mode and blocked in a receive that never asked whether its process was
dying. M20 had measured it and written a workaround into a check to get
past it. The fix was two calls, one in each trampoline, and one reading
moved from after an entry to before the next. Finding out how many other
ways into user mode there were, and proving the list closed, was the
milestone.

### 24.1 The Questions

**Is the trampoline the right place to look?**

Yes. The falsification clause said that if reading the mark there is
unsafe, because the thread is in kernel mode on its own stack outside
the kernel's exclusion, then the mark would have to be read on the far
side at the first entry the thread makes, and a thread killed before it
ever calls anything could not be reached at all. That would have been a
smaller milestone and a worse system.

Ending a thread from a trampoline neither faulted nor hung. What the
measurement found instead is that the kernel lock is not held there: all
2557 arrivals at the two trampolines in a boot found it free, because a
dispatch is made with interrupts off and not with the lock. So the
reading takes the lock when this core does not already hold it, which is
also what orders it against the kill, and the other branch is counted so
that the day something first-dispatches a thread from inside the kernel
the line says so.

**How many ways into user mode are there?**

Three, and the third is not a return from anything. The interrupt path
and the fault path return through a trap, the system call path returns
through a trap, and a thread that has just been made runs a trampoline
in kernel mode and drops into user mode without having trapped. Section
10.5 named the two trap paths and said the mark is read "where a trap
returns to user mode", which covered two of three.

That makes the set of threads a kill has to reach a closed set and the
doors out of it countable, which is what the compared report now says:

```
  threads a kill had to reach: 81, and all of them ended
  by one of three doors: 54 a trampoline, 22 an entry boundary, 4 a trap, 1 already leaving
```

The four numbers come from four places and nothing is a remainder. The
fourth is not a door: it is a thread already inside its own exit when
the mark went down.

**Does a kill reach a thread that has never run?**

Yes, and the supervisor is told 365 to 509 microseconds after asking,
against never. Stage one asserted the wrong answer on purpose, so that a
milestone with no subject would be abandoned rather than built, and
stage two turned both of its assertions over: the kill reaches the
thread, it ends at a trampoline, and it starts no entry at all.

Fifty-four threads in a boot are now ended that way, 53 of them a
program's first thread and one a thread a program made.

**Does a marked thread start an operation?**

No. The reading moved from the end of an entry to before the next one,
which is the same point for every entry but the first and a different
one for the first. Twenty-two threads a boot are stopped there. The
change is also what makes a kill orderable: with the question asked
before the entry, a kill written under the kernel lock and an entry
taken under the same lock have two outcomes and no third.

**Does a kill reach every state at once?**

Yes. Four mechanisms end a thread and each had only ever been checked on
a process with one thread in one state. `fourways` holds all four at
once, computing on the other core, ready and never run, blocked
receiving, and inside a kernel operation, and one kill ends all four
with the kill's code in about 4.3 milliseconds including the join. At
Tier 0 the same lines read zero pokes, because nothing of the target is
running when the killer is, and the poke is not tested there.

**And is a thread made in a process that is over?**

No, and the answer is wider than the milestone asked for. The refusal
covers a process that was killed and a process that ended on its own,
which is two ways to be over and only the first was in the plan. Two
threads a boot are refused with `SYS_ERR_OWNER_DEAD`, one of them to a
process that was never marked at all.

**Does M20's workaround come out?**

Yes. The restart loop no longer connects to its server and sends it a
request before killing it. It kills a server whose thread is ready and
has never run, 52 times, and each round asserts that the count of
programs killed before ever running went up by exactly one, so the loop
cannot quietly go back to measuring the case that already worked.

### 24.2 What It Cost

**Sixteen commits, twenty-one files, 3672 lines added and 282 removed**,
of which 2599 are code, 1053 are documentation and twenty are the
compared reports.

**Two thirds of the code is the measurement.** `init_main.c` accounts
for 1818 of those lines against 234 in `kern_proc.c`, 97 in
`kern_thread.c`, 85 in `kern_syscall.c`, 67 in `kern_channel.c`, 33 in
`kern_timeline.c` and 101 across two headers. Three programs were
written for it: `fourways` at 188 lines, `lastborn` at 100 and `twostep`
at 66. The mechanism is two calls in two trampolines, one reading moved,
one flag on a thread, and a refusal in `proc_thread_create`.

**About 25 kilobytes of text**, 429220 to 455090 on riscv64 at Tier 0
and 570068 to 595260 on aarch64 at Tier 2, almost all of it the checks.

**112 bytes of bss** at every configuration: six counters and the flags
on a thread.

**Five lines in the compared report** where there was one, and the one
that was there moved from 68 kills written to 72.

**No measurable boot time.** The burst session was 8.30 to 8.78 seconds
on riscv64 at Tier 0 before and 8.26 to 8.51 after, and 10.04 to 10.21
on aarch64 at Tier 2 before and 10.16 to 10.25 after. The lock taken at
every one of 2557 first dispatches is inside that spread, measured
separately at five runs either side and not separable from four tenths
of a second of host noise.

### 24.3 What the Building Kept Finding

**A per-port trap path that saved state it did not restore.** The most
serious defect this milestone found is not in anything it built.
`el0_irq` on aarch64 saved `elr_el1` and `spsr_el1` on entry and never
restored them, so a user thread interrupted while the kernel went on to
take another exception returned to the wrong place. It was found from a
symptom that made no sense, a thread whose body is `for(;;) n++`
exiting with status 0, and chased with a ring buffer of exits keyed on
the thread's stack. About five failures in 150 paced runs before, in
three different shapes, and none in 70 after. `el1_irq` restored them
and carried no warning saying why; it does now.

Nothing found it in five milestones of two-core checks, because until
this one no check asserted what a user thread that was interrupted went
on to do.

**Counts that were not measurements.** Three times, one per stage from
four to seven. "4 of 4" was the constant four printed twice. "ended" was
a count of what the walk found rather than of threads that ended.
"already leaving" was the total minus the other three, which adds back
up whatever either side is and therefore says nothing. Each was fixed by
counting at the site, and in the third case that meant a flag set by the
three places that read the mark and by nothing else. The numbers did not
move, which is what says the remainder had been right.

This is the same finding as M20's "assertions that could not fail" and
it arrived three more times in one milestone. The rule it leaves behind
is narrower than that one: a number printed beside other numbers must
come from its own counter, because a sum whose last term is a
subtraction is not a check.

**Kernel entry points called without the lock.** A kernel thread holds
none of the kernel's exclusion, and four calls that a kernel thread
makes did not take it: `timeline_wait`, the three channel wrappers, and
`thread_cancel`. The first cost a real lost wake. `timeline_wait` read
the timeline, found it short, and joined the waiter list while the other
core wrote the value and walked that list, which showed up as a join
that waited thirty seconds for a program that had already exited, three
times in forty runs. Taking the lock made it zero in forty.

The sweep that followed found the rest. What it did not close is
`proc_kill` called straight from a kernel thread, where the mark is
ordered by nothing, because `proc_kill` calls `sched_undefer` and making
it take the lock is not a change to make in passing.

**Reading the state before the moment rather than at it.** Stage one
read the target's state before the kill and never after it, so the
thread could be dispatched on the other core in between and the check
would have passed while measuring the case that works. Stage two read
the mark and then took the lock, which is two cores each storing and
then loading, the one shape that can leave both reading the old value.
Stage three read a channel's sender queue with nothing held. This
milestone's *Watch for* clause named exactly this and it still happened
three times, which says that "assert the state at the moment of the
kill" is a rule that has to be applied per reading rather than per
check.

**A thread's stack outliving the thread.** The slot went back before the
switch had left the thread, so the other core could take the slot while
this one was still running on the stack under it. It appeared as
`unhandled trap in nudge: page, cause=0xc pc=0x0`. A thread now carries
whether the switch has left it, and is parked when it dies rather than
when it is reapable.

**A thread created into the wrong process.** `thread_alloc` attaches the
new thread to the caller's process, which is right for every caller that
existed and wrong for a supervisor making a thread in someone else's
process. It was found by the check that needed that construction and
not by anything else.

**Blocking calls inside a deadline loop, and pulses read as requests.**
Two check-shaped defects that are worth recording because both made a
check say the wrong thing rather than fail: a receive that blocks means
the deadline around it can never fire, and a pulse arrives through the
same `channel_recv` as a request, so a check that expected eight bytes
got a pulse and said the makings were the wrong size.

### 24.4 What Is Still Untested

**A first dispatch from inside the kernel.** The trampoline takes the
lock when this core does not already hold it, and the count of arrivals
that found it held is zero in every boot. That branch exists because the
contract says so, and removing it fails no check.

**The reading before the first entry of a submission.** It needs a
thread that arrived at the kernel already marked, which takes a mark
written while the thread is in user mode and then a trap of the thread's
own within the few microseconds before the kill's interrupt lands. A
program written to make it likely was hit once in eight attempts, once
in sixteen and once in sixty-four, which is a rate that reports the host
rather than the kernel. It is not in the boot.

**A kill written by a kernel thread, ordered against the mark.** Every
kill a program makes is written under the kernel lock, and one check in
M17 calls `proc_kill` from a kernel thread with interrupts off and
nothing else. Against that caller the trampoline's acquire orders
nothing. This is the same residue M20 stage three recorded.

**The reentrancy guard.** A thread interrupted inside a kernel operation
is still not ended there, and nothing constructs that thread. What ends
in this milestone's fourth state is a thread blocked inside an
operation, which is a different thing.

**More than one poke, more than two cores, and real hardware.** A poke
is one inter-processor interrupt per running thread of the target, and
the boot has at most one running thread per target. Every count here
comes from `-smp 2` under an emulator.

**The door accounting is a statement, not a trap.** The invariant with
teeth is that every thread a kill had to reach ended, and anything that
breaks it leaves a thread running, which a join notices first. What the
split of doors adds is that a new path into user mode added without a
reading would show up as a thread that ended its own way. That is
something the boot says about itself rather than something that fires
before the damage.

---

## 25. Milestone 22, in Retrospect

M22 set out to replace a field that counts to one. A receiving thread
recorded the client of its last rendezvous, and four milestones of
accounting read that record: section 12.3's chain walk, M18's
departure notices, M20's channel lifetime, and M21's kill accounting.
Each had been checked against a server with one outstanding request,
because that is the only server the boot had. The console already had
two. The fix is a list; finding out what those four say when the
number is two was the milestone.

### 25.1 The Questions

**Does a receiving thread ever owe more than one?**

Yes, and before anything was built. Stage one measured the tree as it
stood: the console's request thread holds a read with no line to
return, receives again, and owes two. Nineteen times in a paced boot a
thread held a request and blocked receiving, and the record it was
about to give away was still owed every time.

The number is small and it is not an accident of this boot. It is
section 12.6's dispatcher, arrived at by a driver that had to hold a
request open, and nothing in the kernel had a place to put the second
client.

**Does the record name the wrong client?**

Yes. Five records a boot are written over while the client they name
is still owed, and twenty replies a boot come from a thread whose
record named somebody else. The second number is section 12.2 working
as specified, which is why nothing had noticed: a reply is addressed
by identifier and any thread of a server may send it.

**Does the donation go back at the first reply rather than the last?**

It did. `undonate` was documented as running "now that it owes nobody
anything" and ran when the thread replied to whoever it had most
recently received from. A thread holding a request from a client at 24
and answering one at 21 went to its base priority with the first
client still waiting.

It now recomputes from what is left: the highest priority on the set,
and the base only when the set is empty. Four recomputes a boot stop
above base rather than at it. The case is not reachable from the
shell, where every program inherits one priority, so the boot builds
it: a server at 15 owing 24 and 21, answering 21, and still at 24.

**Does a thread inside requests on two channels break the lists?**

It would have, and the fix was to stop asking the question of the
thread. The serving entry is the request now, not the server: a
channel names the clients standing in it, each client names the thread
that owes it, and a thread inside requests on two channels is on both
lists because the two entries are two different clients. One link
field per client is enough where one per thread was not.

That is the milestone's one structural change, and everything after it
was a consequence: the deadline path had to unlink the entry, the exit
had to assert there was none, and `channel_reply`'s free had to ask
the client rather than itself.

**Is a channel freed under a client waiting on it?**

Not any more, and the count says the case is real: two slots a boot
are kept because a request is standing in them and nothing else names
them. The reply that finishes the request gives the slot back in the
same breath.

And a request that ends because its client died takes its entry with
it, seventeen times a boot. That number was not visible before this
milestone, because what left the channel's list was the server and the
server was still there.

**Does a death reach every client?**

It does now. An exit walked the record and released one client; the
others waited out their own deadlines for a reply that could only have
come from the thread that had just gone. The walk reads the set, and
two clients a boot are released by one death, both told `STALE` in
about 830 microseconds where the second used to be told `TIMEOUT` a
second later.

**And does the set cost more on the rendezvous than it buys?**

No, which is the milestone's own falsification clause answered. A
rendezvous against a set of n walks n-1 entries: the request being
answered is at the head, so the unlink finds it without a step, and
what is walked is whatever was there before it. A server owing one
walks nothing at all, which is every server in this tree but the
console and the checks.

Measured as a duration, two hundred round trips against a set of one
take 17629 to 17903 microseconds and against a set of two 19068 to
19573. The 1740 microseconds between them are spent inside the
cross-check this milestone added, timed from within, which leaves
nothing for the pointer step that this can resolve.

The answer the clause would have forced instead was to refuse a
receive on a thread that still owes a reply, and to move the console's
held read to another thread. That would have withdrawn section 12.6's
dispatcher rather than supporting it.

### 25.2 What It Cost

**Fifteen commits, ten files, 3507 lines added and 182 removed**, of
which 2390 are code, 1097 are documentation and twenty are the
compared reports.

**Two thirds of the code is the measurement.** `init_main.c` accounts
for 1524 of those lines against 760 in `kern_channel.c`, 55 in
`thread.h`, 42 in `channel.h` and nine across `subr_pool.c` and
`pool.h`. The mechanism is a count, two pointers, and four functions
that keep them: take, drop, recompute, and the walk that checks them
against each other.

**About 12 kilobytes of text** at Tier 0 on riscv64, 455090 to 466940,
and 18 at Tier 2 on aarch64, 595260 to 613140. Almost all of it is
checks.

**1024 bytes of bss** at Tier 0 and 1040 at Tier 2, of which 512 is
the set itself: sixteen bytes on every thread, across a pool of
thirty-two. The rest is twenty counters and the statics of five
constructions.

**Seven lines in the compared report**, where the milestone before
this one added five.

**No measurable boot time.** The burst session was 8.26 to 8.45
seconds on riscv64 at Tier 0 before and 8.35 to 8.50 after, and 9.98
to 10.50 on aarch64 at Tier 2 before and 9.95 to 10.06 after. That
contains the four hundred round trips stage seven added, about forty
milliseconds of them, and does not separate from the host.

### 25.3 What the Building Kept Finding

**A field that changed owner and kept its name.** Stage four moved
`t_serve_ch` from the server to the client, and left two readers
behind. The first was found in the stage: the path that gives up at a
deadline no longer removed the entry, which surfaced thousands of
lines later as a channel walk reporting a list that named a free slot.
The second was found by the next stage's review: `channel_reply` read
its own `t_serve_ch` to decide which channel might now be free, and a
server's is empty, so the question went unasked for every reply in a
boot. Two hundred replies with the server's field set zero times and
the client's set 191.

Nothing leaked, because the client asks the same question when it
comes back out of `channel_send`. A guarantee had quietly become
somebody else's to keep, which is the shape to watch for: a rename the
compiler cannot help with.

**Walks holding nothing, twice.** Stage one's check walked the thread
pool with interrupts off on one core while the other was inside a
rendezvous. Stage six found the same thing in the kernel: a thread
ended from a syscall holds the kernel lock and a kernel thread calling
`thread_exit` holds nothing, which is 69 of the exits in a boot and
four of the exits that owe anybody. That hole was older than the
stage; what the stage did was make the unlocked region longer and give
it more to touch.

That is the second milestone running to find a kernel entry point
reached without the lock from a kernel thread. M21 found four of them
and wrote the rule down; this one found a fifth by asking the question
of a path M21 had not.

**Instruments that changed what they measured.** Stage two's walk ran
inside the window `intr_region_report` measures, so the boot's longest
interrupts-off region became the check rather than the kernel: 404
microseconds against a 708 microsecond region. Moving it after the
report and making it one pass took it to 205 and gave the region back.
Stage seven's two runs differed in two things, the set depth and two
hundred priority recomputes the first run paid for and the second did
not, which cancelled and made the cost look like noise. Both are the
same error: a measurement that includes its own apparatus.

**Guards that hid what they were meant to catch.** `owed_drop` refused
to go below zero rather than saying it had been asked to, which turns
a count that has gone wrong into one that reads as though it had not.
It is a panic now, and dropping a client twice says so. The same
milestone's overwrite test compared two counters that could both be
right for the wrong reason, and was replaced by asking whether the
record's client is still owed.

**Falsifications that fire somewhere else.** The *Watch for* clause
said to expect this and it happened twice. Stage two's unbounded walk,
broken on purpose, hung inside M21 stage five's check rather than
failing in its own. Stage five's donation falsification fired stage
three's assertion first, because the same code serves both and stage
three's construction runs earlier; reaching stage five's own assertion
needed stage three's removed. Both are written down as what they are,
which is the point of naming the shape in advance.

**A check that had to stop running to be checked.** A server at the
priority of its highest client never gives the core to the boot
thread, so a check that spins waiting for the boot thread to do
something waits for ever. It blocks on a timeline the boot signals
instead. M20 stage five's review names the same shape from the other
end.

**And a substitution that landed in the wrong function.** A `perl`
anchor matched inside a `#if SYS_TIER == 2` block, which compiled at
Tier 0 because the block was preprocessed out, and was found only by
building Tier 2. Anchor on unique text, and build both tiers after a
patch applied by pattern.

### 25.4 What Is Still Untested

**A dispatcher.** Nothing in this tree receives on one thread and
replies from another pool of workers, which is the shape section 12.6
describes and this milestone makes expressible. What exercises the set
is the console, which owes two, and five constructions written for the
checks. The claim that the kernel now supports the shape rests on the
pieces, not on a server built that way.

**More than two owed at once.** The high-water mark is two for the
whole boot, and the milestone's own *Watch for* clause named this: two
is also what an off-by-one would print. The list walks are bounded by
the thread pool and panic on overrun, so a longer set would be caught
if it happened, but nothing here makes one.

**A recompute that reaches another core's run queue.** The rule from
section 11.4 says a READY thread belongs to the core whose queue it is
on, and the recompute skips and counts rather than reaching across. A
probe never fired in six Tier 2 runs. The branch is reasoned, not
observed, and the counter in the compared report reads zero.

**A client whose deadline fired while its server exits.** The exit
walk has three cases and the boot reaches two of them. Removing the
third changes nothing in any run, because the window between a timer
wake and the client running has never contained a server's exit.

**A pointer to a slot that was given away.** The exit takes every
client off the set on the reasoning that the thread's slot is about to
be somebody else's. The slot is freed at the reap and section 12.5
reaches those clients first, so the boot has never produced the
dangling pointer the invariant exists to prevent. What it has is the
assertion that says so.

**Replies the record did not name, as a compared number.** It moves
with console pacing: twenty in a paced run and none in a burst one,
because a burst session always has a line waiting and the console
never holds a read. It is reported above the compared line for that
reason, and the milestone's first stage learned it by asserting it
above zero and stopping the burst run.

**How the check publishes what it measured.** Every construction here
writes its results and then sets a flag the boot thread spins on, with
nothing ordering the two. The emulation will not reorder them and the
convention is the file's rather than this milestone's, but nothing
here makes it safe.

**And the usual.** Two cores under an emulator, no hardware, and every
duration the right shape and the wrong magnitude.

---

## 26. Bring-Up Order Within M1

M1 is large enough to need its own sequence. Each stage produces something
testable, and a stage that fails, fails visibly.

**Stage 1. Boot to a known state.** Take the machine, set up a stack,
initialise the object pools, spin. Nothing to test but that the image runs,
which is worth confirming before anything depends on it.

**Stage 2. One thread, no scheduler.** Build the thread object and the context
switch. Switch between two threads that yield to each other explicitly. This is
where register save and restore gets debugged, in the simplest setting it will
ever be in.

**Stage 3. The scheduler.** Ready queue, priorities, preemption. Test with
several compute-bound threads at different priorities and confirm the highest
runnable one runs.

**Stage 4. Handles and the trap.** The handle table and the operation entry
point. A no-op operation is the first one worth having: it exercises the entire
entry, validation, status-write and return path with no other machinery
involved.

**Stage 5. Timelines.** Create, signal, wait, and the error state. Timelines
come before IPC because interrupts and timers both land on them, and because
they are simpler to get right in isolation.

**Stage 6. Interrupts.** Attach an interrupt to a timeline and drive it from a
real device, the timer being the obvious first one. At this point the system
responds to hardware.

**Stage 7. Timers.** Periodic and one-shot on top of stage 6.

**Stage 8. IPC and spawn.** Channels, send, receive, reply, then priority
inheritance. Process creation, handle inheritance, the startup record. The
driver process and the file read close the slice here.

**One note on order.** Timelines before IPC is the choice most likely to feel
wrong, since IPC seems more fundamental. It is not. Interrupts and timers
depend on timelines and not on message passing, so timelines first gets the
system responding to hardware several stages earlier.

---

## 27. Ordering: What Is Forced and What Is Chosen

Worth separating, because the forced edges are not negotiable and the chosen
ones are.

**Forced.** M2 after M1, since a scheduler running two programs needs the
message passing they rendezvous over. M3 after M2, since a shell that cannot
spawn a process is not a shell. M6 after M4, since a cohort without protection
domains is a naming convention. M7 after M6, since cohort recovery is the first
mechanism that cannot be demonstrated without death, and M7 not before M2,
since nothing earlier has anything to reclaim. M9 after M3, since measuring a
system with no workload measures nothing. M10 after M6, since issuing ops need
a device that does DMA.

**Chosen, and reversible.** M3 before M4. The argument is that the MMU
milestone's real test is running the same software on both tiers, which needs
software. The counter-argument is that porting less code to Tier 2 is easier,
which would put M4 first. If M3 grows larger than expected, invert them.

Also chosen: M7 after M6 rather than between M4 and M5. Death could be built
as soon as faults exist, and the reason not to is that M5 and M6 gain nothing
from it while paying for it. If either turns out to need a process to die and
be replaced before it can be demonstrated, M7 moves ahead of it and nothing
else changes.

**Independent.** M5 is pure userland and libc and blocks nothing, so it can
move anywhere after M3. M8 is almost entirely kernel and shares little with M5,
so the two can proceed in parallel if there is ever reason to.

---

## 28. What Would Change This Plan

Each of these is a plausible outcome, not a worry. The plan is arranged so that
they surface early and cheaply.

**Timelines do not earn their place (M1).** Remove the object, keep blocking
receive, and section 9 collapses. This is the cheapest thing on the list to
discover and the most disruptive to the document, since fences run through
interrupts, timers, exit and the submission engine.

**Compound requests do not pay (M2).** *Answered: they do.* Three
rendezvous become one and the connection pool goes from one allocation to
none, the second being the structural saving. Section 25.7 stands, with an
entry-index field and a close entry removed from it that building it found
to be wrong. Had it gone the other way, 25.7 would have been deleted and
section 12.7 with it.

**One thread per source is unaffordable (M3).** Wait-sets come forward from
`PROPOSALS.md`. The queue model, not the array model, and only after evaluating
whether a timeline enqueuing a coalesced pulse on a channel is sufficient.

**The interface differs between tiers (M4).** The thesis is wrong. Part I is
rewritten and the project needs a different reason to exist.

**Namespaces are unworkable (M5).** Either the mount table moves, or the design
concedes an ambient root. Sections 20 and 25 both change.

**Cohort faults are intolerable (M7).** Cohorts drop to a naming convention and
zero-copy goes through ordinary grants, at the cost the design was trying to
avoid.

**The submission engine does not pay (M10).** It is deleted. Section 23 already
defines the calling convention around a single operation for exactly this
reason, so nothing else moves.

**Substitution does not pay (M11).** *Answered: not in counts.* A chain
that carries a connection in a register saves the fixed cost of a call
multiplied by one fewer than the number of entries, and nothing per
entry, which is the same law M10 measured for batching without
dependencies. What it buys is that the batch can be written at all. The
register file stays, because the cost of expressing a dependency turned
out to be nothing; had it been more than nothing, section 17.4 would
have gone and section 23 is arranged so that removing it costs nothing
else.

---

## 29. Deliberately Not Scheduled

Named here so that they stay named rather than drifting in.

- A GDB remote stub over the debug UART of section 22.4. Named there as the
  companion to the debug console, and deliberately unspecified, because a
  stub written against a real debugging session is worth more than one
  designed in advance. It arrives with the board that needs it.
- Everything in `PROPOSALS.md`, until its own trigger fires.
- Conformance testing, certification, and any statement about what an
  implementation must demonstrate to be Nyctos.
- Hardware ports beyond QEMU `virt`. Real boards bring firmware handover,
  interrupt controller variation, clock and PHY bring-up, and cache maintenance
  for non-coherent DMA. None of it is interesting until the system works on the
  emulator.
- Writing any of this up as teaching material, and the per-process isolation
  aim that section 1.4 of `design.md` describes. Both are long-term reasons
  the system is built the way it is, and both constrain the code today. The
  isolation aim in particular adds no work, because it is to be reached with
  mechanisms already designed; if it ever appears to need a new one, the aim
  is re-examined rather than the design extended. Neither is a deliverable.
